Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a
split reductive group over $k$ with Borel $B\supseteq T$, base
$\Delta=\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I}$ and fundamental weights $\omega_i$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]],
[[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). For every $i\in I$ there exist
a finite-dimensional rational representation $V_i$ of $G$ and a primitive vector
$v_i\in V_i$ whose weight $\lambda_i$ satisfies
$$\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=0\ (j\ne i),\qquad \langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0.$$
When the root datum is semisimple,
$\lambda_i=\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\omega_i$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ with Weyl
group $W$ and root datum $(X,\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$, $X=X(T)$, and let
$B\supseteq T$ be a Borel subgroup with system of positive roots $\Phi^+$ and
base $\Delta$
([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). For a rational
representation $(V,r)$ of $G$
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) the
$T$-weight decomposition is $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in X}V_\chi$ with
$V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\}$
([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]]); the
**weights** of $(V,r)$ are the characters $\chi$ with $V_\chi\ne0$, and
$V_\chi$ is the **weight space** of $\chi$. An element $\lambda\in X$ is
**dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$ for every
$\alpha\in\Phi^+$ (equivalently, for every $\alpha\in\Delta$); write $X^+$ for
the set of dominant weights. Define a partial order on $X$ by $\lambda\ge\mu$ if
and only if
$\lambda-\mu=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The **fundamental weights** $\omega_i$
($i\in\Delta$) are the elements of $X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ dual to the
simple coroots, $\langle\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=\delta_{ij}$; they form a
basis of the weight lattice part and every $\lambda\in X\otimes\mathbb Q$
decomposes as
$\lambda=\sum_i\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\omega_i+\lambda_0$ with
$\lambda_0$ pairing to $0$ with every coroot
([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]).

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Its **root datum** is the quadruple
$$R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\Phi^\vee(G,T)),$$
where the character and cocharacter lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], the roots are the nonzero adjoint characters, and $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ consists of the associated coroots. Its **rank** is $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}X(T)=\dim T$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, its base $\Delta(B)$ consists of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots; the pair gives the based root datum $(R(G,T),\Delta(B))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the root-group, Weyl and centre suppliers for the following structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The coroots supplied by [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]] are in bijection with the roots and satisfy $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. This quadruple is a reduced root datum in the sense of [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], its Weyl group is canonically $W(G,T)$, and $\Delta(B)$ is a base whose nonnegative integral combinations recover $\Phi^+(B)$ ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Its semisimple rank is $|\Delta|=\operatorname{rank}G-\dim Z(G)$, and $G$ is semisimple exactly when $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X(T)$ ([[lem-reductive-center-radical-and-semisimple-quotient]]).

The isomorphism class of the unbased root datum is independent of the split Borel pair, but it is not asserted to have a unique abstract isomorphism: Weyl automorphisms already refute that assertion in type $A_1$. For two fixed split Borel pairs $(B,T),(B',T')$, conjugation by $g\in G(k)$ carrying the first pair to the second induces a canonical comparison of their **based** root data. If $g'$ is another such element, $g^{-1}g'$ lies in $N_G(B)\cap N_G(T)=B\cap N_G(T)=T$, by Borel self-normality and the Weyl/Borel correspondence. Conjugation by $T$ acts trivially on its character and cocharacter lattices and preserves the root-coroot labels, so the two induced comparisons agree. Thus uniqueness applies to the comparison attached to the fixed based pairs, while the unbased datum is defined up to isomorphism class. ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-cartan-subgroups-conjugacy-and-density]])

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a reductive algebraic group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]) and let $T$ be a maximal torus of $G$. Then: (a) $Z(G)\subseteq T$ for every maximal torus $T$, and $Z(G)$ is of multiplicative type ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]]); (b) $R(G)=Z(G)_t$ is the largest subtorus of $Z(G)$ (not the full possibly nonreduced neutral component), its formation commutes with every extension of the base field, and the quotient $G/R(G)$ is semisimple; (c) $G/Z(G)$ has trivial centre; (d) the semisimple rank of $G$ equals $\operatorname{rk}G-\dim Z(G)$; (e) with $G'$ the derived subgroup ([[def-derived-subgroup-and-solvable-algebraic-group]]), $Z(G)_t\cap G'$ is finite, $G=Z(G)_t\cdot G'$ and the multiplication map $Z(G)_t\times G'\to G$ is surjective with finite kernel, and $G'$ is semisimple; (f) $G$ is semisimple iff $R(G)=1$ iff $Z(G)$ is finite. The quotient $G/R(G)$ is the represented normal affine quotient ([[thm-nonaffine-affine-normal-group-quotient-affine]]); it is smooth and connected by [[lem-nonaffine-exact-group-sequence-affine-smooth-connected-properties]].

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

derivations.claim: Since $G$ is semisimple, its root datum is semisimple and the annihilator $X_0$ is zero by [F3].

Apply [F1] with $j=i$: there exist a finite-dimensional rational representation $V_i$ and a primitive vector $v_i\in V_i$ of weight $\lambda_i$ with $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_k^\vee\rangle=0$ for $k\ne i$ and $d:=\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0$. By [F2] the element $\lambda_i$ decomposes as $\lambda_i=\sum_j\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\omega_j+(\lambda_i)_0$ with $(\lambda_i)_0\in X_0$; by step 1.1 the term $(\lambda_i)_0$ vanishes and all coefficients except the $i$-th are zero, so $\lambda_i=d\omega_i$.
Therefore $d>0$, $d\omega_i=\lambda_i\in X(T)$, and $d\omega_i$ is the weight of the primitive vector $v_i$ in the finite-dimensional rational representation $V_i$ of $G$.

The descent statement is Milne 22.12: the centre $Z(G')$ acts through $\lambda+Q$, so $N\subseteq Z(G')$ acts trivially exactly when $\lambda$ vanishes on $N$, i.e. when $\lambda\in X(T)$; the action then factors through the finite-locally-free quotient $G=G'\!/N$ by its universal property.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The adjoint representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a rational representation, so $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak t=\operatorname{Lie}(T)=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ and the **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_\alpha\neq0$ ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal subtorus of $\ker\alpha$, of codimension one in $T$, $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, the subgroup attached to the cyclic semigroup of positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ by [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]]; $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$ ([[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]). The **Weyl group** of the pair is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ ([[lem-fixed-loci-and-centralizers-of-torus-actions-are-connected]]). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the system of **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, with $-\Phi^+(B)$ the negative roots relative to $B$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]).

The Weyl group is a finite étale group scheme, being the quotient of the normalizer of the torus by the torus itself; it acts faithfully on $X(T)$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). The root groups $U_\alpha$ depend only on the root $\alpha$ and not on the auxiliary cocharacter used in their construction, because the cyclic semigroup $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic: it consists of the positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ that belong to the character lattice, and the subgroup $H_{(\alpha)}$ of [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]] is characterized by its weight semigroup. The positive system of a Borel subgroup determines and is determined by the Borel subgroup: two Borels containing $T$ yield the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne, Ch. 21), a fact used in the proof of the Weyl-group theorem.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a reductive algebraic group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]) and let $T$ be a maximal torus of $G$. Then: (a) $Z(G)\subseteq T$ for every maximal torus $T$, and $Z(G)$ is of multiplicative type ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]]); (b) $R(G)=Z(G)_t$ is the largest subtorus of $Z(G)$ (not the full possibly nonreduced neutral component), its formation commutes with every extension of the base field, and the quotient $G/R(G)$ is semisimple; (c) $G/Z(G)$ has trivial centre; (d) the semisimple rank of $G$ equals $\operatorname{rk}G-\dim Z(G)$; (e) with $G'$ the derived subgroup ([[def-derived-subgroup-and-solvable-algebraic-group]]), $Z(G)_t\cap G'$ is finite, $G=Z(G)_t\cdot G'$ and the multiplication map $Z(G)_t\times G'\to G$ is surjective with finite kernel, and $G'$ is semisimple; (f) $G$ is semisimple iff $R(G)=1$ iff $Z(G)$ is finite. The quotient $G/R(G)$ is the represented normal affine quotient ([[thm-nonaffine-affine-normal-group-quotient-affine]]); it is smooth and connected by [[lem-nonaffine-exact-group-sequence-affine-smooth-connected-properties]].

A group scheme of finite type over a field $k$ is **of multiplicative type** if it is fpqc locally diagonalizable: there is a faithfully flat quasi-compact covering $S'\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ on which it becomes a diagonalizable group. A **torus** over $k$ is a finite-type group scheme fpqc locally isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$, for a finite integer $r\ge0$. A group or torus is **split** if the relevant isomorphism already exists over $k$.

Diagonalizable means the group-algebra construction in [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]. These definitions include the trivial torus of rank zero and nonsmooth multiplicative-type groups. No affineness or separable splitting condition is imposed by definition. Affineness and field splitting are proved locally on this page, followed by finite separable splitting.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ for which the adjoint weight space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ in $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}G$ is nonzero. The adjoint action is rational, and the weight decomposition
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$$
is the choice-free decomposition into character eigenspaces ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). This nonzero-weight definition uses no choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the following supplemental structural facts and subgroup constructions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The reductive centralizer identity $C_G(T)=T$ and Lie fixed-point equality give $\mathfrak g_0=\operatorname{Lie}T=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ ([[thm-chevalley-centralizer-radical-and-reductive-centralizers]], [[lem-lie-functor-exactness-fixed-points-and-generation]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$, put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)_t=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal reduced subtorus of its kernel, of codimension one in $T$, and $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$. The **root group** is $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, attached to the semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ in $X(T)$; it is smooth connected unipotent and $T$-stable with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$. Its identity-concentrator construction takes place in $G_\alpha$, not in all of $G$ ([[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]], [[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]).

The **Weyl group** is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$. Under the stated AC premise it is a finite étale group scheme and acts faithfully on $X(T)$ (Milne21.1 and21.12). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}B\}$ and negative roots $-\Phi^+(B)$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]], [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). Root groups are independent of the auxiliary cocharacter because $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic and its smooth connected subgroup is characterized by its specified Lie weight subspace. Two Borels containing $T$ give the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne21.23 and21.35). These structural facts inherit the explicit AC premise; the definition of a root as a nonzero adjoint character above remains choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
simple rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ with Borel
subgroup $B\supseteq T$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]], [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a)
$V$ contains a primitive vector $v$, and it is unique up to multiplication by a
nonzero scalar; (b) its weight $\lambda$ is dominant and the weight space
$V_\lambda=kv$ is one-dimensional; (c) every weight $\mu$ of $V$ satisfies
$\mu\le\lambda$, i.e. $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\ge0$; (d) any two primitive vectors of $V$ have the same weight; this
weight is called the **highest weight** of $V$.

For every field $k$, $X(D_k(M))=M$ via $m\mapsto e_m$, and $\operatorname{Hom}(D_k(M),D_k(N))=\operatorname{Hom}(N,M)$ naturally. Moreover $k[M]$ is finitely generated as an algebra if and only if $M$ is finitely generated. For $M\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$, one has $D_k(M)\cong\mathbf G_m^r\times\prod_i\mu_{n_i}$, where $\mu_n=\operatorname{Spec}k[t]/(t^n-1)$.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then the character group $X(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,\mathbf G_m)$ is canonically isomorphic to $M$, the cocharacter group $X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,T)$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual lattice $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, and the pairing $X(T)\times X_*(T)\to\mathbb Z$, $(\chi,\lambda)\mapsto\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle$, defined by $\chi\circ\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,\mathbf G_m)=\mathbb Z$, is a perfect $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing identifying $X_*(T)$ with $X(T)^\vee$. Both lattices are free of finite rank equal to $\dim T$, and the identifications and the pairing commute with extension of scalars. In particular $X(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and $X_*(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces in perfect duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the sheafification and represented-sheaf
suppliers used below. Work on a fixed big fppf site of $k$-schemes as in Stacks
Section 34.7. Let $k$ be a field, and let $s,t:R\to U$ be two morphisms of
$k$-schemes with common target ([[def-morphism-of-schemes]]); such a pair is a
**pre-relation** on $U$.

The **naive quotient presheaf** $P_{U/R}$ is the functor on the category of
$k$-schemes sending a $k$-scheme $T$ to the quotient of the set $U(T)$
([[def-fibre-product-schemes-universal-property]]) by the equivalence relation
generated by $\{(s(x),t(x)):x\in R(T)\}$; its value at $T=\operatorname{Spec}k$
is the set of $k$-points of $U$ modulo the relation generated by $R(k)$. In
general $P_{U/R}$ is only a presheaf
([[def-presheaf-representable-functor-and-representation]]).

An **fppf sheaf** on this category is a presheaf $F$ such that for every
$k$-scheme $T$ and every fppf covering family $\{T_i\to T\}$ — a set-indexed
family of flat morphisms locally of finite presentation which is jointly
surjective onto $T$ ([[def-faithfully-flat-morphism-schemes]],
[[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) — the diagram
$F(T)\to\prod_iF(T_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}F(T_i\times_TT_j)$ is an
equalizer. The **fppf quotient sheaf** $U/R$ is the sheafification of
$P_{U/R}$ for this topology: a morphism $P_{U/R}\to U/R$ of presheaves with
$U/R$ an fppf sheaf, initial among morphisms from $P_{U/R}$ to fppf sheaves.
Every representable presheaf is an fppf sheaf
([[lem-nonaffine-fppf-descent-of-scheme-morphisms]]); a $k$-scheme $M$
**represents the quotient sheaf** $U/R$ when there is a natural isomorphism
$h_M\cong U/R$
([[def-presheaf-representable-functor-and-representation]]), and then $M$ is
unique up to unique isomorphism.

For a group scheme $G$ of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]])
acting on $U$ one takes $R=G\times_kU$ with $s$ the second projection and $t$
the action morphism, and writes $U/G$; for $U=G$ and a closed subgroup scheme
$H\subseteq G$ ([[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]) acting by right
translation one takes $R=G\times_kH$, $s(g,h)=g$, $t(g,h)=gh$, and writes
$G/H$. The natural map from the naive quotient presheaf to its quotient sheaf is
generally not an isomorphism; sheafification can both identify sections that
agree locally and introduce sections that only have local representatives. The
orbit set is only $P_{U/R}(k)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $R=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be affine finite-type $k$-schemes, and let
$s,t:R\to U$ be finite locally free morphisms
([[def-faithfully-flat-morphism-schemes]]) such that $j=(t,s):R\to U\times_kU$
is an equivalence relation. Put $C=\{a\in A: s^\sharp(a)=t^\sharp(a)\}$
([[def-quotient-sheaf-and-representable-quotient]] for the quotient sheaf
$U/R$). Then $C$ is a finite-type $k$-algebra, the morphism
$U\to M=\operatorname{Spec}C$ is finite locally free and surjective, the
canonical morphism $R\to U\times_MU$ is an isomorphism, and $M$ represents the
fppf quotient sheaf $U/R$.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then the character group $X(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,\mathbf G_m)$ is canonically isomorphic to $M$, the cocharacter group $X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,T)$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual lattice $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, and the pairing $X(T)\times X_*(T)\to\mathbb Z$, $(\chi,\lambda)\mapsto\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle$, defined by $\chi\circ\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,\mathbf G_m)=\mathbb Z$, is a perfect $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing identifying $X_*(T)$ with $X(T)^\vee$. Both lattices are free of finite rank equal to $\dim T$, and the identifications and the pairing commute with extension of scalars. In particular $X(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and $X_*(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces in perfect duality.

For every field $k$, $X(D_k(M))=M$ via $m\mapsto e_m$, and $\operatorname{Hom}(D_k(M),D_k(N))=\operatorname{Hom}(N,M)$ naturally. Moreover $k[M]$ is finitely generated as an algebra if and only if $M$ is finitely generated. For $M\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$, one has $D_k(M)\cong\mathbf G_m^r\times\prod_i\mu_{n_i}$, where $\mu_n=\operatorname{Spec}k[t]/(t^n-1)$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$. If a closed subgroup scheme $H\subseteq G$ ([[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]) is both unipotent ([[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]]) and diagonalizable ([[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]), then $H=1$. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the geometric splitting and closed-subgroup conversion, consequently a torus contains no nontrivial unipotent closed subgroup, and the intersection of a unipotent subgroup with a torus is trivial. No smoothness of $H$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ of separated finite-type $k$-group schemes with scheme kernel $K$, its scheme-theoretic image $I$ is isomorphic to the represented fppf quotient $G/K$. The map $G\to I$ is faithfully flat of finite presentation. If $G$ is affine, smooth, or connected, respectively, so is $I$. If $q:G\to Q$ is an exact quotient and $N\subset G$ a closed normal subgroup, the image of $N\to Q$ is normal in $Q$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup, $U=B_u$, $W=N_G(T)/T$, and choose representatives $n_w\in N_G(T)(k)$ ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) the double cosets $Bn_wB$ depend only on $w$, are smooth locally closed subvarieties of $G$, and $G$ is their disjoint union, $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}Bn_wB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}U^wn_wB$; (b) for every $w$ the multiplication map $U^w\times B\to Bn_wB$ is an isomorphism, and $G/B=\bigsqcup_wY(w)$ with $Y(w)=UwB/B\cong\mathbf A^{n(w)}$ an affine space of dimension $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|$; (c) the **big cell** $B^-B=U^-TB$ (with $B^-$ the opposite Borel, $B^-\cap B=T$ and $U^-=B^-_u$) is open and dense in $G$, the multiplication map $U^-\times T\times U\to G$ is an open immersion, the open dense longest Bruhat cell is $Bn_{w_0}B=n_{w_0}(B^-B)$, a translate of this opposite big cell. Its flag cell $Y(w_0)$ is the unique flag cell of maximal dimension $|\Phi^+|$, while the group cell has dimension $\dim G$; (d) on $k$-points, $G(k)=\bigsqcup_wB(k)wB(k)$ is the Bruhat decomposition attached to the Tits system of [[lem-simple-reflection-double-coset-rule]], and the $G(k)$-orbits on $G/B\times G/B$ are in bijection with the $B(k)$-double cosets of $G(k)$, hence indexed by $W$.

A **split reductive group** over $k$ is a pair $(G,T)$ consisting of a reductive algebraic group $G$ over $k$ ([[def-radical-and-unipotent-radical-of-an-algebraic-group]]) and a maximal torus $T\subseteq G$ that is split, i.e. isomorphic over $k$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r$ ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]). 

The following supplemental existence and field-invariance facts assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) through their cited suppliers. Since maximal tori exist, any torus lies in one, and maximality is preserved by field extension ([[lem-maximal-tori-extension-conjugacy-and-derived-group]]), the rank $\dim T$ and the semisimple rank $\operatorname{rk}(G/R(G))$ are well defined. A homomorphism of split reductive groups $(G,T)\to(G',T')$ is a homomorphism of algebraic groups carrying $T$ into $T'$. Because $G$ is affine of finite type, the adjoint representation $\operatorname{Ad}:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{\mathfrak g}$ ([[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]], [[thm-lie-bracket-and-adjoint-action-from-infinitesimals]]) restricts to a rational representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, to which the eigenspace decomposition of diagonalizable groups applies ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]]). We write $X=X(T)$, $X^\vee=X_*(T)$ for the lattices of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]. Every reductive group splits over a finite separable extension of the base field; the split hypothesis is kept throughout.

Under this same assumption, the rank of $(G,T)$ is the common dimension of its maximal tori and the semisimple rank is the rank of the semisimple quotient $G/R(G)$; both are additive invariants of the pair. The split hypothesis is exactly the requirement that the character lattice $X(T)$ be a free $\mathbb Z$-module with trivial Galois action, which is why the root datum of $(G,T)$ is defined over $k$ rather than only over a finite extension. A homomorphism of split reductive groups need not carry $T$ isomorphically onto $T'$; the induced map on character lattices is then only a homomorphism. An isogeny carrying $T$ onto $T'$ induces an injective character-lattice map with finite cokernel, by the split character anti-equivalence ([[lem-diagonalizable-character-antiequivalence]]); it need not induce an isomorphism even if the two groups have the same abstract root datum. For example, the isogeny $t\mapsto t^p$ of $\mathbf G_m$ in characteristic $p$ induces multiplication by $p$ on its character lattice $\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: For (a), first inclusion: let $R$ be a $k$-algebra and let $z\in Z(G)(R)$. By [F1] $z\in T(R)$. Since $z$ is central, $z\,u_\alpha(c)\,z^{-1}=u_\alpha(c)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$ and every $c\in R$, while the conjugation formula of [F2] gives $z\,u_\alpha(c)\,z^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(z)c)$. As $u_\alpha$ is an isomorphism of group schemes, $u_\alpha(R)$ is injective, so $\alpha(z)c=c$ for all $c$; setting $c=1$ gives $\alpha(z)=1$. Hence $z\in(\bigcap_{\alpha\in\Phi}\ker\alpha)(R)$ and $Z(G)\subseteq\bigcap_{\alpha\in\Phi}\ker\alpha$.

Conversely let $t\in(\bigcap_\alpha\ker\alpha)(R)$. By [F2], conjugation by $t$ is the identity on $T_R$ and each $U_{\alpha,R}$, so it is the identity on the base-changed root big cell of [F8]. Restriction $O(G)\to O(U^-\times T\times U)$ is injective because this is a dense open in an integral affine scheme. Tensoring that injection with the $k$-vector space $R$ preserves injectivity: each finite tensor expression can be checked in a finite-dimensional subspace of $R$, where the map is a finite direct sum of the original injection. Thus restriction remains injective even for nonreduced $R$, and the two endomorphisms $c_t$ and $\operatorname{id}$ of $G_R$ have equal maps on coordinate rings. Hence $t$ is central. This proves the scheme equality in (a); the same argument works for split reductive groups.

The restriction $\pi|_{T'}:T'\to T$ is, by [F6], a finite locally free surjection of split tori with kernel $N$, so it identifies $T$ with the fppf quotient $T'/N$ [F5]. Hence a character $\chi\in X(T')$ vanishes on $N$ if and only if it factors through $T'/N=T$, i.e. if and only if $\chi\in X(T)\subseteq X(T')$: a character trivial on $N$ is constant on $N$-orbits and factors through the quotient by its universal property, while a character pulled back from $T$ is trivial on $N$.

The root groups, rather than the total Lie differential, give the root correspondence. For $\alpha'\in\Phi'$, the kernel of $\pi|_{U_{\alpha'}}$ is $N\cap U_{\alpha'}$. It is unipotent as a subgroup of $U_{\alpha'}\simeq\mathbf G_a$ and diagonalizable as a subgroup of $T'$, so it is trivial by [F7]. The restriction is therefore an isomorphism onto a smooth connected closed image $H\simeq\mathbf G_a$. Centrality of $N$ and the root conjugation formula imply $\alpha'|_N=1$, so step 1.3 gives a unique character $\alpha\in X(T)$ whose pullback is $\alpha'$. The image $H$ is $T$-stable and its nonzero tangent line has weight $\alpha$, so $\alpha$ is a root of $G$. The root-subgroup containment criterion of [F2] then gives $U_\alpha\subseteq H$; both are smooth connected curves, hence $H=U_\alpha$. Distinct $\alpha'$ give distinct $\alpha$ by injectivity of torus pullback. Since the isogeny preserves dimension and torus rank, and $\dim G=\dim T+|\Phi|$, this injection of roots is bijective. For compatible Borels, it identifies the positive roots: the image of $B'$ is the Borel generated by $T$ and the images of its positive root groups. Rank-one normalizer representatives map to the corresponding target reflections, so torus pullback intertwines the two reflections. Comparing their formulas gives $\langle\pi^*x,\alpha'{}^\vee\rangle=\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for every $x\in X(T)$, and hence $\pi_*\alpha'{}^\vee=\alpha^\vee$. This includes inseparable isogenies and nonreduced $N$.

For the second assertion of (a), apply [F4] to the morphism $\psi=(\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Phi}:T\to\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbf G_m$. Its kernel is $\bigcap_\alpha\ker\alpha=Z(G)$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2, and its dual $\psi^*:\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z e_\alpha\to X(T)$ sends $e_\alpha$ to $\alpha$, so its image is exactly the root lattice $Q$. Therefore $X(Z(G))=\operatorname{coker}\psi^*=X(T)/Q$, and the restriction map $X(T)\to X(Z(G))$ is the quotient map with kernel $Q$.

For (b): let $\mu$ be a weight of $V$. By [F3] applied to the split reductive group $(G,T)$, one has $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with $m_\alpha\ge0$; hence for $z\in Z(G)(R)$ we get $\alpha(z)=1$ for all roots $\alpha$ by step 1.1, so $\mu(z)=\lambda(z)\prod_\alpha\alpha(z)^{-m_\alpha}=\lambda(z)$. The action of $z$ on the spanning weight spaces $V_\mu\subseteq V_R$ is therefore the scalar $\lambda(z)$, so $z$ acts on $V_R$ as $\lambda(z)\operatorname{id}$. This is the character of $Z(G)$ obtained by restricting $\lambda\in X(T)$, which under step 2.1 corresponds to $\lambda+Q\in X(T)/Q=X(Z(G))$.

The argument of steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 used only that the group is split reductive (generation by $T$ and the root groups, the conjugation formula, the weight description of simple modules, and [F1]), so it applies verbatim to the split reductive group $(G',T')$: $Z(G')=\bigcap_{\alpha'\in\Phi'}\ker\alpha'$ with $X(Z(G'))=X(T')/Q'$, and $Z(G')$ acts on a simple $G'$-module of highest weight $\lambda$ through the character $\lambda+Q'$.

Now let $\lambda\in X(T')$ and let $V'$ be a simple $G'$-module of highest weight $\lambda$. By step 4.1 the centre $Z(G')$ acts on $V'$ through $\lambda+Q'$; since $N\subseteq Z(G')$ by [F6] and $Q'$ vanishes on $Z(G')$, the subgroup $N$ acts on $V'$ through the character $\lambda|_N$. Hence $N$ acts trivially if and only if $\lambda|_N=1$, which by step 1.3 is exactly $\lambda\in X(T)$. If $N$ acts trivially, the $G'$-action factors through the fppf quotient $G'/N=G$ [F5], and the resulting $G$-module is simple because every $G$-submodule is a $G'$-submodule; conversely, if $V'$ factors through $G$, then $N$ acts trivially, so $\lambda\in X(T)$. It remains to identify the highest weight: by [F3] applied to $(G',T')$, the $T'$-weights of $V'$ are $\lambda-\sum_{\alpha'\in\Delta'}m_{\alpha'}\alpha'$ with $m_{\alpha'}\ge0$ and $\lambda$ has multiplicity one, and by the root correspondence of step 1.4 the roots $\alpha'$ are pullbacks of the roots $\alpha$ of $(G,T)$ with the same positive systems; hence the $T$-weights of the descended module are $\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$, again with $\lambda$ of multiplicity one. So the descended $G$-module is simple with highest weight $\lambda$.

operations.old_value: A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha}\ker\alpha$, and a **base** is a subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition; the lattice form, not the Euclidean one, is what is attached to a split reductive group in [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]].

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $X$ be a separated $k$-scheme of finite type with a locally affine action of $\mathbf G_m$ and let $Z\subseteq X$ be a $\mathbf G_m$-stable closed subscheme ([[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then the concentrator functor $R\mapsto\{x\in X(R): \lim_{t\to0}tx\text{ exists and lies in }Z(R)\}$ is representable by a closed subscheme $X(Z)\subseteq X$; the inclusion $X(Z)\hookrightarrow X$ is a local immersion and the limit morphism $p:X(Z)\to Z$ is affine. If $X$ and $Z$ are smooth, then $X(Z)$ is the unique smooth closed subscheme of $X$ whose geometric points are the $x$ with $\lim_{t\to0}tx\in Z(k^{\mathrm a})$. The construction and the pair $(X(Z),p)$ commute with extension of the base field and with $\mathbf G_m$-equivariant morphisms, and for the conjugation action of $\mathbf G_m$ on a smooth group $G$ the scheme $G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g=e\})$ is a normal algebraic subgroup of $P_G(\lambda)$.

Let $X$ be a separated $k$-scheme of finite type with an action of $\mathbf G_m$ ([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]), and let $Z\subseteq X$ be a $\mathbf G_m$-stable closed subscheme. For a morphism $\varphi:\mathbf G_m\times_k X_0\to X$, the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\varphi(t)$ exists if $\varphi$ extends to a morphism $\mathbf A^1\times X_0\to X$, in which case the extension and its value at $0$ are unique by separatedness; for a point $x\in X(R)$ one writes $tx$ for the orbit map and asks that $t\mapsto tx$ extend over $\mathbf A^1_R$. When $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, the action is a $\mathbb Z$-gradation $A=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_n$ and $\lim_{t\to0}tx$ exists iff $f_n(x)=0$ for all $f_n\in A_n$ with $n<0$; the **concentrator subscheme** $X(Z)$ is the closed subscheme defined by the ideal generated by $A_0\cap\mathfrak a+\sum_{n<0}A_n$, where $\mathfrak a=\ker(A\to A(Z))$ is the graded ideal of $Z$. The associated functor sends $R$ to the set of $x\in X(R)$ with $\lim_{t\to0}tx\in Z(R)$.

The uniqueness in the first sentence is the valuative separatedness of [[def-separated-scheme-over-base]] applied to the two extensions over $\operatorname{Spec}R[t]$ and $\operatorname{Spec}R[t^{-1}]$ glued along $\operatorname{Spec}R[t,t^{-1}]$ ([[def-morphism-of-schemes]]); the affine description is the gradation induced by the coaction of $k[t,t^{-1}]$ on $A$ when $X$ is affine ([[def-affine-scheme]]), and the closed subscheme structure is that of the ideal sheaf generated by the listed homogeneous pieces ([[def-ideal-sheaf]]). The functor-of-points description of $X(Z)$ is stated here and proved in [[thm-concentrator-subscheme-representability-and-smoothness]]; no representability is asserted by the definition itself.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $S$ be a torus acting on a connected group variety $G$ over $k$. Then the fixed-point subgroup $G^S=C_G(S)$ is smooth and connected and $\operatorname{Lie}(G^S)=\mathfrak g^S$; consequently, for any torus $S\subseteq G$ the centralizer $C_G(S)$ is smooth and connected, and for a maximal torus $T$ of $G$ the Cartan subgroup $C_G(T)$ is smooth, connected and nilpotent with $C_G(T)=N_G(C_G(T))^\circ$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]). If $S\subseteq B$ for a Borel subgroup $B$ of $G$, then $C_G(S)\cap B$ is a Borel subgroup of $C_G(S)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let $T$ be a maximal torus. Then Chevalley's theorem holds: $R_u(G)=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B_u)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $R_u(G)\cdot T=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the intersections running over the finite set of Borel subgroups containing $T$. Consequently, for any torus $S$ in $G$ one has $R_u(C_G(S))=R_u(G)\cap C_G(S)$, and for a torus $S$ acting on $G$ one has $R_u(G^S)=R_u(G)^S$. In particular, if $G$ is reductive, then $C_G(S)=G^S$ is smooth, connected and reductive for every torus $S\subseteq G$, and $C_G(T)=T$ for every maximal torus $T$ of a reductive $G$.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes, let $x\in X$ and put $s=f(x)$.
The morphism $f$ is **smooth at $x$** when the following three conditions hold
at $x$:

1. $f$ is locally of finite presentation at $x$
   ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]);
2. $f$ is flat at $x$ ([[def-flat-morphism-schemes]]);
3. the scheme-theoretic fibre $X_s$ ([[def-geometric-fibre]]) is
   geometrically regular at $x$, that is, for every field extension
   $K/\kappa(s)$ the local ring of $X_s\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)}
   \operatorname{Spec}K$ at every point over $x$ is regular
   ([[def-ag-geometrically-regular-algebra-and-fibre]]).

The morphism $f$ is **smooth** if it is smooth at every point of $X$. A
morphism with empty source is smooth vacuously, and no condition is imposed
by an empty fibre: the pointwise clause of the definition is quantified over
primes of the fibre, of which there are none.

Smoothness is a condition on the germ of $f$ at $x$, so it is preserved by
restricting the source to an open neighbourhood of $x$ and by shrinking the
target to an open neighbourhood of $s$; affine-locally it becomes a condition
on a finitely presented ring map at a prime, and the equivalence with the
formal lifting and Jacobian formulations is proved on this page, not assumed
here. Relative dimension is defined separately, and in relative dimension
zero smoothness is equivalent to étaleness later on this page.

derivations.claim: Apply the concentrator construction of [F1] to the conjugation action on $X=G$ and the closed subscheme $Z=G$: the functor represented is exactly $R\mapsto\{g\in G(R):\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\}$, and its representing object is a closed subscheme $P_G(\lambda)\subseteq G$, the fibre over the identity of the limit morphism $p:P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is $U_G(\lambda)$, and the intersection of the loci where the limits at $0$ and at $\infty$ exist is the fixed locus of the action, i.e. $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=G^{\mathbf G_m}=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))=Z_G(\lambda)$. Smoothness of the three groups when $G$ is smooth follows from [F1] and [F3]: $Z_G(\lambda)$ is a fixed locus of a torus action, and $P_G(\lambda)$, $U_G(\lambda)$, being the concentrator and the fibre of its limit map over the smooth point $e$, are smooth; by uniqueness of the smooth model over $k^{\mathrm a}$ they are the unique smooth subgroups with the stated geometric points. The multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism of group schemes: on the tangent space it is the direct-sum decomposition of the nonnegative weight part of $\mathfrak g$ into its positive and zero weight pieces, and on geometric points every $g$ with a limit factors uniquely as $u\cdot z$ with $u$ in the fibre over $e$ and $z$ fixed by the action. The open immersion $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is the Luna-type decomposition: an element of $G$ whose orbit map extends to $0$ lies in $P_G(\lambda)$, and every element sufficiently close to th...

Assume $G$ reductive. The quotient $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)\cong Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ is reductive by [F3]. Since $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected, normal and unipotent in $P_G(\lambda)$, it is contained in $R_u(P_G(\lambda))$; conversely $R_u(P_G(\lambda))$ maps into the reductive group $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)$ as a connected normal unipotent subgroup, hence to the identity, so $R_u(P_G(\lambda))\subseteq U_G(\lambda)$. Therefore $R_u(P_G(\lambda))=U_G(\lambda)$, and the quotient is reductive.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $X$ be a separated $k$-scheme of finite type with a locally affine action of $\mathbf G_m$ and let $Z\subseteq X$ be a $\mathbf G_m$-stable closed subscheme ([[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then the concentrator functor $R\mapsto\{x\in X(R): \lim_{t\to0}tx\text{ exists and lies in }Z(R)\}$ is representable by a scheme $X(Z)$; its realization morphism $i:X(Z)\to X$ is a local immersion and the limit morphism $p:X(Z)\to Z$ is affine. If $X$ and $Z$ are smooth, then $X(Z)$ is smooth and $i$ identifies its geometric points with the indicated limit locus. If $X$ is affine, $i$ is a closed immersion; if $X$ and $Z$ are also smooth, $X(Z)$ is the unique smooth closed subscheme with that locus. The construction and the pair $(X(Z),p)$ commute with extension of the base field and with $\mathbf G_m$-equivariant morphisms, and for the conjugation action of $\mathbf G_m$ on a smooth affine group $G$ the scheme $G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g=e\})$ is a normal algebraic subgroup of $P_G(\lambda)$.

Let $X$ be a separated $k$-scheme of finite type with an action of $\mathbf G_m$ ([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]), and let $Z\subseteq X$ be a $\mathbf G_m$-stable closed subscheme. For a morphism $\varphi:\mathbf G_m\times_k X_0\to X$, the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\varphi(t)$ exists if $\varphi$ extends to a morphism $\mathbf A^1\times X_0\to X$, in which case the extension and its value at $0$ are unique by separatedness; for a point $x\in X(R)$ one writes $tx$ for the orbit map and asks that $t\mapsto tx$ extend over $\mathbf A^1_R$. When $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, the action is a $\mathbb Z$-gradation $A=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_n$ and $\lim_{t\to0}tx$ exists iff $f_n(x)=0$ for all $f_n\in A_n$ with $n<0$; the **concentrator subscheme** $X(Z)$ is the closed subscheme defined by the ideal generated by $A_0\cap\mathfrak a+\sum_{n<0}A_n$, where $\mathfrak a=\ker(A\to A(Z))$ is the graded ideal of $Z$. The associated functor sends $R$ to the set of $x\in X(R)$ with $\lim_{t\to0}tx\in Z(R)$.

The uniqueness in the first sentence is the valuative separatedness of [[def-separated-scheme-over-base]] applied to the two extensions over $\operatorname{Spec}R[t]$ and $\operatorname{Spec}R[t^{-1}]$ glued along $\operatorname{Spec}R[t,t^{-1}]$ ([[def-morphism-of-schemes]]); the affine description is the gradation induced by the coaction of $k[t,t^{-1}]$ on $A$ when $X$ is affine ([[def-affine-scheme]]), and the closed subscheme structure is that of the ideal sheaf generated by the listed homogeneous pieces ([[def-ideal-sheaf]]). The functor-of-points description of $X(Z)$ is stated here and proved in [[thm-concentrator-subscheme-representability-and-smoothness]]; no representability is asserted by the definition itself.

Let $G$ be an affine finite-type group scheme over an arbitrary field $k$. Every right comodule over its coordinate Hopf algebra $A=k[G]$ is the filtered union of its finite-dimensional subcomodules. The right regular representation of $G$ on $A$ contains a finite-dimensional subrepresentation $V$ such that $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is a closed immersion. These assertions allow nonreduced $G$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be a diagonalizable group over $k$, so that $O(G)=k[M]$ for an abelian group $M$ with group-like basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$ ([[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then every rational representation $(V,\rho)$ of $G$ ([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) decomposes as
$$V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in M}V_\chi,\qquad V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\},$$
a direct sum over the characters $\chi\in X(G)=M$ of $G$ of the corresponding eigenspaces. The eigenspaces may have arbitrary multiplicities. The decomposition is choice-free and is inherited by subrepresentations, quotients and the middle terms of extensions. In finite dimension, choosing finite bases of the nonzero eigenspaces expresses a representation as a finite direct sum of one-dimensional character representations; in particular $G$ is linearly reductive. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the same character-line decomposition holds in arbitrary dimension by [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]; only this last assertion uses arbitrary choice.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-lie-algebra-of-a-group-scheme]]), and let $H,H_1,H_2$ be algebraic subgroups. (a) For a finite inverse system $(G_i)$ of algebraic groups, $\operatorname{Lie}(\varprojlim G_i)\cong\varprojlim\operatorname{Lie}(G_i)$; in particular $\operatorname{Lie}$ is left exact on exact sequences and $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\times_G H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\times_{\operatorname{Lie}(G)}\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$, so if $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ then $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\cap H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$ ([[lem-lie-algebra-tangent-space-and-functoriality]]). (b) If $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, $H$ is smooth and $G$ is connected, then $H=G$; if the Lie algebras of smooth subgroups $H_1,\dots,H_n$ generate $\mathfrak g$ as a Lie algebra and $G$ is connected, then the $H_i$ generate $G$. (c) If $H$ acts on $G$ by conjugation, then $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(H))=\mathfrak g^H$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(N_G(H))/\operatorname{Lie}(H)=(\mathfrak g/\operatorname{Lie}(H))^H$; in particular $\dim C_G(H)\le\dim\mathfrak g^H$, with equality iff $C_G(H)$ is smooth.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then the character group $X(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,\mathbf G_m)$ is canonically isomorphic to $M$, the cocharacter group $X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,T)$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual lattice $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, and the pairing $X(T)\times X_*(T)\to\mathbb Z$, $(\chi,\lambda)\mapsto\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle$, defined by $\chi\circ\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,\mathbf G_m)=\mathbb Z$, is a perfect $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing identifying $X_*(T)$ with $X(T)^\vee$. Both lattices are free of finite rank equal to $\dim T$, and the identifications and the pairing commute with extension of scalars. In particular $X(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and $X_*(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces in perfect duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let $T$ be a maximal torus. Then Chevalley's theorem holds: $R_u(G)=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B_u)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $R_u(G)\cdot T=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the intersections running over the finite set of Borel subgroups containing $T$. Consequently, for any torus $S$ in $G$ one has $R_u(C_G(S))=R_u(G)\cap C_G(S)$, and for a torus $S$ acting on $G$ one has $R_u(G^S)=R_u(G)^S$. In particular, if $G$ is reductive, then $G^S$ is smooth, connected and reductive for every torus action by group automorphisms, in particular $C_G(S)$ has these properties for every torus $S\subseteq G$, and $C_G(T)=T$ for every maximal torus $T$ of a reductive $G$.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes, let $x\in X$ and put $s=f(x)$.
The morphism $f$ is **smooth at $x$** when the following three conditions hold
at $x$:

1. $f$ is locally of finite presentation at $x$
   ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]);
2. $f$ is flat at $x$ ([[def-flat-morphism-schemes]]);
3. the scheme-theoretic fibre $X_s$ ([[def-geometric-fibre]]) is
   geometrically regular at $x$, that is, for every field extension
   $K/\kappa(s)$ the local ring of $X_s\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)}
   \operatorname{Spec}K$ at every point over $x$ is regular
   ([[def-ag-geometrically-regular-algebra-and-fibre]]).

The morphism $f$ is **smooth** if it is smooth at every point of $X$. A
morphism with empty source is smooth vacuously, and no condition is imposed
by an empty fibre: the pointwise clause of the definition is quantified over
primes of the fibre, of which there are none.

Smoothness is a condition on the germ of $f$ at $x$, so it is preserved by
restricting the source to an open neighbourhood of $x$ and by shrinking the
target to an open neighbourhood of $s$; affine-locally it becomes a condition
on a finitely presented ring map at a prime, and the equivalence with the
formal lifting and Jacobian formulations is proved on this page, not assumed
here. Relative dimension is defined separately, and in relative dimension
zero smoothness is equivalent to étaleness later on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be a smooth algebraic
group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) acting on
a separated finite-type $k$-scheme $X$
([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]), and let
$x\in X(k)$ ([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]). Then the
orbit subscheme $O_x$ is locally closed in $X$ and stable under $G$, and the
orbit map $\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is faithfully flat and locally of finite
presentation. In particular $O_x$ is smooth over $k$ and of finite type. The
Axiom of Choice is used exactly as in the generic-flatness and constructibility
inputs below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the represented-sheaf and geometric suppliers
used on this page. Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be a group scheme of finite type
over $k$ acting on a separated finite-type $k$-scheme $X$
([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]), let
$x\in X(k)$, and let $H$ be a closed subgroup scheme of $G$
([[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]) with $H=G_x$
([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]). Assume the orbit map
$\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is faithfully flat and locally of finite presentation,
where $O_x$ is the orbit subscheme. Then $O_x$ represents the fppf quotient
sheaf $G/H$ ([[def-quotient-sheaf-and-representable-quotient]]), the quotient
morphism is $\varrho_x$, and the kernel-pair morphism
$G\times_kH\to G\times_{O_x}G$, $(g,h)\mapsto(g,gh)$, is an isomorphism.

derivations.claim: The affine graded concentrator construction [F1] represents $P=P_G(\lambda)$ and the identity concentrator $U=U_G(\lambda)$ as closed subschemes of $G$. Conjugation acts by group automorphisms, so the limit of a product or inverse is the product or inverse of the limits, on every base algebra. Thus $P$ is a subgroup and its limit map $p:P\to G$ is a homomorphism. Its image lies in the fixed subgroup $Z=Z_G(\lambda)$, since a limit at zero is fixed; $p|_Z=\operatorname{id}$ and $U=\ker p$ is normal. Limits in both directions force every nonzero graded coefficient to vanish, giving $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z$ scheme-theoretically. Fixed smoothness [F3] gives smooth $Z$, while [F1] applied to smooth $G$ with targets $G$ and $\{e\}$ gives smooth $P,U$. Their smooth geometric-point models are unique by [F1].

Embed $G$ in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ by [F2] and choose a weight basis in which $\lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t^{m_1},\ldots,t^{m_n})$, $m_1\ge\cdots\ge m_n$. In $\mathrm{GL}(V)$, conjugation multiplies entry $x_{ij}$ by $t^{m_i-m_j}$. Thus $P_{\mathrm{GL}(V)}$ has zero entries when $m_i-m_j<0$, $Z_{\mathrm{GL}(V)}$ has zero entries for nonzero differences, and $U_{\mathrm{GL}(V)}$ has identity diagonal blocks and zero entries unless $m_i-m_j>0$. These descriptions hold over every algebra. The corresponding groups for $G$ are their scheme intersections with $G$, since the orbit limit in the ambient group lies in closed $G$. Applying the intersection formula for Lie and the dual-number entry calculation gives $\operatorname{Lie}P=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$, $\operatorname{Lie}Z=\mathfrak g_0$, and $\operatorname{Lie}U=\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$.

Multiplication $U\rtimes Z\to P$ has the explicit inverse $g\mapsto(gp(g)^{-1},p(g))$. The first component has limit identity and the second is fixed; both maps are scheme morphisms and satisfy the inverse identities on every algebra. This proves the semidirect product as a group-scheme isomorphism, without inferring it merely from tangents and geometric points.

Put $U^-=U_G(-\lambda)$. The weight-block equations give $U^-\cap P=1$ on every algebra. Let the smooth group $U^-\times P^{\mathrm{op}}$ act on $G$ by $(u,p)\cdot g=ugp$; its scheme stabilizer at identity is therefore trivial. After algebraic closure, [F4] identifies its orbit map $\mu:U^-\times P\to G$ with an isomorphism onto a locally closed orbit. Its differential at identity is addition $\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r\oplus\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g$, an isomorphism by step2.1. Between these smooth schemes this is the étale criterion at identity (the invertible Jacobian calculation in Milne13.33's proof). Translations by the acting group carry this calculation to every point of the domain; hence the locally closed orbit immersion is étale and therefore open. Open immersion descends along the faithfully flat field extension, so $\mu$ is the asserted open immersion over $k$. The graded limit action extends to $\mathbf A^1\times U\to U$ and sends $\{0\}\times U$ to identity. Over the algebraic closure every point is connected to identity by that affine-line morphism, so $U$ is geometrically connected, even for disconnected $G$. Its weight-block matrices lie in an upper-unitriangular group, making it unipotent by [F5].

If $G$ is reductive, [F3] makes $Z=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ reductive. By step3.1 the quotient $P/U$ is $Z$, and $U$ is smooth connected normal unipotent by step4.1. Thus $U\subseteq R_u(P)$; the image of $R_u(P)$ in reductive $Z$ is a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup and is trivial. Consequently $R_u(P)=U$, proving the full reductive clause. All preceding assertions allow disconnected smooth affine $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric and smooth-local suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group variety over $k$ equipped with an action by automorphisms of a split torus $T$, and let $\Psi=\Psi(G,T)\subseteq X(T)$ be the weights of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}G$. Then:

(a) For every subsemigroup $A\subseteq X(T)$, there is a unique $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety $H_A\subseteq G$ with
$$\operatorname{Lie}H_A=\bigoplus_{\chi\in A\cap\Psi}\mathfrak g_\chi.$$
Every $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety whose Lie algebra is contained in this subspace is contained in $H_A$. No finite generation, saturation, exclusion of $0$, or strictly definite cone condition is imposed on $A$.

(b) For a nonzero weight $\alpha$, let $(\alpha)$ be the semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ lying in $X(T)$, and let $\lambda$ be a cocharacter with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0$. Put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)_t$, the largest reduced subtorus of its kernel, and $G_\alpha=G^{T_\alpha}$, the fixed subgroup for the given external action. Then $H_{(\alpha)}=U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)$, the identity concentrator for this action on $G_\alpha$; it is smooth connected unipotent and $T$-stable, with Lie algebra the sum of the strictly positive rational-$\alpha$ weight spaces. Every $T$-stable **smooth** subgroup variety $H\subseteq G$ with $\operatorname{Lie}H\supseteq\operatorname{Lie}H_{(\alpha)}$ contains $H_{(\alpha)}$. The smoothness qualification is necessary: $\alpha_p\subseteq\mathbf G_a$ with the scaling torus has the same Lie algebra as $\mathbf G_a$, but does not contain that positive-weight subgroup.

(c) The closed subgroup generated by two $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup varieties $H_1,H_2$ is smooth connected, and its weight semigroup is generated by their weight semigroups. Here a weight semigroup means the semigroup of nonempty finite sums of Lie weights; the empty weight set generates the empty semigroup. If $H_1,H_2$ generate $G$, this identifies the weight semigroup of $G$.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth algebraic group over $k$ and let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a cocharacter, acting on $G$ by $t\cdot g=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]] for the notation, [[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then $P_G(\lambda)=G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\})$, $Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ (the fibre of $g\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g$ over $e$) are algebraic subgroups of $G$, with $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ normal in $P_G(\lambda)$; over $k^{\mathrm a}$, $P_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ are the unique smooth subgroups whose geometric points are the $g$ with the indicated limits. If $G$ is smooth, then $P_G(\lambda),Z_G(\lambda),U_G(\lambda)$ are smooth; the multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism; $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is an open immersion; $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected and unipotent; and under the weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the $\mathbf G_m$-action one has $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}U_G(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$. If moreover $G$ is reductive, then $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)\cong Z_G(\lambda)$ is reductive and $R_u(P_G(\lambda))=U_G(\lambda)$.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then the character group $X(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,\mathbf G_m)$ is canonically isomorphic to $M$, the cocharacter group $X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,T)$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual lattice $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, and the pairing $X(T)\times X_*(T)\to\mathbb Z$, $(\chi,\lambda)\mapsto\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle$, defined by $\chi\circ\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,\mathbf G_m)=\mathbb Z$, is a perfect $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing identifying $X_*(T)$ with $X(T)^\vee$. Both lattices are free of finite rank equal to $\dim T$, and the identifications and the pairing commute with extension of scalars. In particular $X(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and $X_*(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces in perfect duality.

A group scheme of finite type over a field $k$ is **of multiplicative type** if it is fpqc locally diagonalizable: there is a faithfully flat quasi-compact covering $S'\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ on which it becomes a diagonalizable group. A **torus** over $k$ is a finite-type group scheme fpqc locally isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$, for a finite integer $r\ge0$. A group or torus is **split** if the relevant isomorphism already exists over $k$.

Diagonalizable means the group-algebra construction in [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]. These definitions include the trivial torus of rank zero and nonsmooth multiplicative-type groups. No affineness or separable splitting condition is imposed by definition. Affineness and field splitting are proved locally on this page, followed by finite separable splitting.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $X$ be a smooth connected variety over $k$ with an action of $\mathbf G_m$ ([[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). (a) **Luna's theorem:** if the action is definite (all weights of the gradation of $\mathcal O_X$ are $\ge0$), then the fixed locus $X^{\mathbf G_m}$ is connected, the limit map $X\to X^{\mathbf G_m}$, $x\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}tx$, exists, and for every $x\in X^{\mathbf G_m}$ the canonical $\mathbf G_m$-equivariant morphism $X\to T_x^+(X)$ into the positive part of the tangent space at $x$ is an isomorphism of varieties; this applies in particular to $X=G$ and to representable homogeneous spaces $X=G/P$. (b) **Bialynicki-Birula:** if $X$ is smooth, connected and complete and $X^{\mathbf G_m}$ is finite and constant, then for each fixed point $x$ there is a unique smooth subscheme $X(x)$ with $X(x)(k^{\mathrm a})=\{y:\lim_{t\to0}ty=x\}$, the tangent space at $x$ is the contracting subspace, $X(x)$ is an affine space, and the underlying topological space of $X$ is the disjoint union of the locally closed subsets $X(x)$; there is a unique attracting fixed point $x^-$ with $X(x^-)$ open dense and a unique repelling fixed point $x^+$ with $X(x^+)=\{x^+\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $S$ be a torus acting on a connected group variety $G$ over $k$. Then the fixed-point subgroup $G^S=C_G(S)$ is smooth and connected and $\operatorname{Lie}(G^S)=\mathfrak g^S$; consequently, for any torus $S\subseteq G$ the centralizer $C_G(S)$ is smooth and connected, and for a maximal torus $T$ of $G$ the Cartan subgroup $C_G(T)$ is smooth, connected and nilpotent with $C_G(T)=N_G(C_G(T))^\circ$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]). If $S\subseteq B$ for a Borel subgroup $B$ of $G$, then $C_G(S)\cap B$ is a Borel subgroup of $C_G(S)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over $k$. Then $G$ is unipotent ([[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]]) if and only if $G_{k^{\mathrm a}}$ contains no nontrivial torus, equivalently if and only if $G$ has rank $0$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]); in particular a connected group variety of rank $0$ is unipotent. Consequently a connected group variety of semisimple rank $0$ is solvable, and a reductive group of semisimple rank $0$ is a torus ([[lem-reductive-center-radical-and-semisimple-quotient]]).

Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be an affine unipotent algebraic group over $k$ ([[def-affine-scheme]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then there is a central series
$$G=G_0\supseteq G_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq G_r=1$$
of closed subgroup schemes of $G$ whose successive quotients are isomorphic to closed subgroup schemes of $\mathbf G_a$. In particular every unipotent algebraic group is nilpotent and hence solvable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. (a) Let $G$ be a connected nilpotent algebraic group over $k$; then $Z(G)_s$, the largest subtorus of the centre, is the largest algebraic subgroup of $G$ of multiplicative type ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]]), it is central and characteristic, and $G/Z(G)_s$ is unipotent ([[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]]); if $G$ is smooth then $Z(G)_s$ is a torus, and over a perfect field the smooth connected nilpotent groups are exactly the products $U\times T$ with $U$ unipotent and $T$ a torus. (b) For a connected group variety $G$ and a torus $S\subseteq G$, the torus $S$ is maximal among the tori of $G$ if and only if $C_G(S)/S$ contains no nontrivial torus.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a connected affine group variety over $k$, i.e. a smooth connected affine algebraic group of finite type over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then: (a) for every Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ the quotient $G/B$ is complete; (b) any two Borel subgroups of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (c) any two maximal tori of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (d) any two Borel pairs are conjugate. The hypotheses connected and smooth, and the algebraic closedness of $k$, are essential; the statements are not claimed over general fields or for nonsmooth groups.
