Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be a diagonalizable group over $k$, so that $O(G)=k[M]$ for an abelian group $M$ with group-like basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$ ([[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then every rational representation $(V,\rho)$ of $G$ ([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) decomposes as
$$V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in M}V_\chi,\qquad V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\},$$
a direct sum over the characters $\chi\in X(G)=M$ of $G$ of the corresponding eigenspaces. The eigenspaces may have arbitrary multiplicities. The decomposition is choice-free and is inherited by subrepresentations, quotients and the middle terms of extensions. In finite dimension, choosing finite bases of the nonzero eigenspaces expresses a representation as a finite direct sum of one-dimensional character representations; in particular $G$ is linearly reductive. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the same character-line decomposition holds in arbitrary dimension by [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]; only this last assertion uses arbitrary choice.

Let $T$ be a split torus over $k$, so that $T\cong D_k(M)$ for a free abelian group $M$ of finite rank ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]], [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]). Then the character group $X(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(T,\mathbf G_m)$ is canonically isomorphic to $M$, the cocharacter group $X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,T)$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual lattice $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, and the pairing $X(T)\times X_*(T)\to\mathbb Z$, $(\chi,\lambda)\mapsto\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle$, defined by $\chi\circ\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathbf G_m,\mathbf G_m)=\mathbb Z$, is a perfect $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing identifying $X_*(T)$ with $X(T)^\vee$. Both lattices are free of finite rank equal to $\dim T$, and the identifications and the pairing commute with extension of scalars. In particular $X(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and $X_*(T)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ are $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces in perfect duality.

A group scheme of finite type over a field $k$ is **of multiplicative type** if it is fpqc locally diagonalizable: there is a faithfully flat quasi-compact covering $S'\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ on which it becomes a diagonalizable group. A **torus** over $k$ is a finite-type group scheme fpqc locally isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$, for a finite integer $r\ge0$. A group or torus is **split** if the relevant isomorphism already exists over $k$.

Diagonalizable means the group-algebra construction in [[def-diagonalizable-group-and-character-module]]. These definitions include the trivial torus of rank zero and nonsmooth multiplicative-type groups. No affineness or separable splitting condition is imposed by definition. Affineness and field splitting are proved locally on this page, followed by finite separable splitting.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ be a nonzero Noetherian local ring of dimension $d$, and let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in\mathfrak m^d$. Then $\mathbf x$ is a regular system of parameters if and only if its classes form a $k$-basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. In particular every lift of a cotangent basis in a regular local ring generates $\mathfrak m$ and is a system of parameters.

The first clause below is choice-free; the second uses the published
Jacobson-radical unit criterion and therefore inherits its Axiom-of-Choice
boundary.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $I\subset R$ be an ideal, and let
$M$ be a finite $R$-module. Put
$$ K:=\bigcap_{n\ge0} I^nM. $$
Then:

1. $K$ is exactly the set of elements $m\in M$ for which $(1-a)m=0$ for some
   $a\in I$;
2. if $I\subseteq J(R)$, then $K=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. A connected separated finite-type $k$-group scheme is geometrically connected. A smooth connected such group is geometrically integral. Every geometrically reduced finite-type $k$-group scheme is smooth.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let a torus $S$ act by group automorphisms on a smooth connected group variety $G$ over $k$. Its fixed subgroup $G^S$ is smooth and $\operatorname{Lie}(G^S)=\mathfrak g^S$. If $G$ is affine, $G^S$ is also connected. In particular, the centralizer $C_G(S)$ of a torus subgroup $S\subseteq G$ is smooth and connected when $G$ is smooth connected affine. For a maximal torus $T$ of such an affine $G$, the Cartan subgroup $C_G(T)$ is smooth connected nilpotent and satisfies $C_G(T)=N_G(C_G(T))^\circ$. If $S\subseteq B$ for a Borel subgroup $B$ of a smooth connected affine $G$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]), then $C_G(S)\cap B$ is a Borel subgroup of $C_G(S)$. For an external action, $G^S$ denotes the fixed subgroup; the notation $C_G(S)$ is reserved for subgroup conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth algebraic group over $k$ and let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a cocharacter, acting on $G$ by $t\cdot g=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]] for the notation, [[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then $P_G(\lambda)=G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\})$, $Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ (the fibre of $g\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g$ over $e$) are algebraic subgroups of $G$, with $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ normal in $P_G(\lambda)$; over $k^{\mathrm a}$, $P_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ are the unique smooth subgroups whose geometric points are the $g$ with the indicated limits. Then $P_G(\lambda),Z_G(\lambda),U_G(\lambda)$ are smooth; the multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism; $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is an open immersion; $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected and unipotent; and under the weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the $\mathbf G_m$-action one has $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}U_G(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$. If moreover $G$ is reductive, then $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)\cong Z_G(\lambda)$ is reductive and $R_u(P_G(\lambda))=U_G(\lambda)$.

derivations.claim:
Decompose $\mathfrak m= igoplus_\chi\mathfrak m_\chi$ by [F1] and let $J_A$ be the ideal generated by $\mathfrak m_\chi$ for $\chi
otin A$. It is a Hopf ideal. For $f\in\mathfrak m_\chi$, the reduced coproduct $\Delta f-f\otimes1-1\otimes f$ belongs to $\mathfrak m\otimes\mathfrak m$ and decomposes into terms of weights $ eta,\gamma$ with $ eta+\gamma=\chi$. If $\chi
otin A$, at least one of $ eta,\gamma$ is outside $A$, so every term vanishes modulo $J_A$ in one factor. The antipode preserves weights and the augmentation ideal, and the counit kills it. Thus $C_A=\operatorname{Spec}(R/J_A)$ is a closed $T$-stable subgroup, and its construction commutes with field extension. Using $\mathfrak m_\chi$, rather than all $R_\chi$, ensures that $1$ is never killed when $0
otin A$.

Choose homogeneous lifts $f_1,\ldots,f_d\in\mathfrak m$ of a weight basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. At identity, [F2] identifies the completed local ring of $G$ with $k[[f_1,\ldots,f_d]]$. A homogeneous element of augmentation weight $\chi$ has only nonconstant monomials of that same weight in its formal expansion: compare coefficients in each finite quotient by powers of the maximal ideal, using the equivariant parameter isomorphism. If $\chi\notin A$, every such monomial involves a parameter whose weight is outside $A$, since $A$ is closed under addition. Conversely those outside-weight parameters themselves generate part of $J_A$. Hence the completed ideal of $J_A$ is exactly the ideal generated by the outside-weight parameters, and the completed local ring of $C_A$ is the power-series ring in the remaining parameters. Ideals in this Noetherian formal power-series ring are closed, so passage from the expansions to this ideal identity is legitimate. The quotient of the smooth local ring by these independent outside-weight parameters is smooth at identity by the coordinate Jacobian criterion in [F2]. Every generator of $J_A$ is zero in its completion, and completion injectivity [F2] makes it zero already in that quotient. Thus the localized $J_A$ is exactly this parameter ideal. Repeat after algebraic closure to conclude that $C_A$ is smooth at identity; translations and [F3] make it smooth everywhere. Its identity component $H_A=C_A^\circ$ is smooth connected and has the displayed Lie algebra.

Let $H$ be a $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup with Lie algebra contained in the selected weights. Its homogeneous formal parameters have weights in $A$. Restrict $f\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ with $\chi\notin A$ to $H$; its expansion contains no nonconstant monomial, since all such monomial weights belong to $A$, and its constant is zero. Thus it vanishes in the completion at identity. Completion injectivity [F2] and geometric integrality [F3] show that it vanishes globally on $H$: localization of its integral coordinate ring at identity is injective. Therefore $H\subseteq C_A$, and connectedness gives $H\subseteq H_A$. If $H$ has exactly the selected Lie algebra, its dimension equals that of $H_A$ by smoothness; a closed proper subgroup of a geometrically irreducible smooth connected group has smaller dimension. Hence $H=H_A$, proving the full uniqueness and containment in(a), including empty and nonsaturated semigroups.

The fixed subgroup $G_\alpha=G^{T_\alpha}$ is smooth connected by [F4], with Lie weights precisely the rational multiples of $\alpha$, including zero. Apply the cocharacter theorem in $G_\alpha\rtimes T$ to $\lambda$. Its identity concentrator lies in the kernel $G_\alpha$ of projection to $T$, since conjugation leaves that projection unchanged. It is smooth connected unipotent and has exactly the strictly positive rational-$\alpha$ Lie weights by [F4]. It is $T$-stable, since the torus action commutes with $\lambda$, and equals $H_{(\alpha)}$ by(a). Now take a smooth $T$-stable $H$ with the asserted Lie containment, possibly disconnected. Its $T_\alpha$-fixed subgroup is smooth, and the identity concentrator there is a smooth connected subgroup of $U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)$, with the same positive Lie space. Smoothness and dimension therefore make it the whole $U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)$, proving containment in $H$. For $H=\alpha_p\subseteq\mathbf G_a$ the smoothness premise fails and the stated counterexample confirms its necessity.

Let $K$ be the closed subgroup generated by $H_1,H_2$. It can be constructed by taking the joint kernel in $O(G)$ of pullbacks under all finite word-product maps with factors $H_i$ (including inverses, which remain in $H_i$). The resulting quotient is jointly injected into their coordinate rings. Tensor joint injectivity follows by restricting a finite tensor expression to finite-dimensional coefficient spans; concatenating words and reversing them show the kernel is a Hopf ideal. After any field extension the word-source rings are reduced, so their jointly injected subalgebra is reduced; thus $K$ is geometrically reduced and smooth. Every word source is geometrically connected. Pullbacks of an idempotent of $O(K)$ are constants equal to its augmentation; joint injectivity therefore makes that idempotent constant. Thus $K$ is connected. The construction is $T$-stable.

For any smooth connected affine $T$-group $L$, the weights occurring in its augmentation ideal are exactly the semigroup generated by its Lie weights. Indeed, a nonzero homogeneous function has a nonzero formal expansion by the injectivity in [F2] and integrality in [F3]; one of its nonconstant monomials expresses its weight as a sum of parameter weights. Conversely, any nonempty finite sum is realized by the product of the corresponding nonzero homogeneous parameter lifts, which is nonzero in the integral ring $O(L)$. Apply this to $K,H_1,H_2$. Any nonzero homogeneous augmentation function on $K$ has a nonzero pullback under some word map by joint injectivity. In the tensor product of the word-source coordinate rings, its weight is a sum of augmentation weights of those factors, with at least one nonconstant factor; it therefore belongs to the semigroup generated by the Lie weights of $H_1,H_2$. Conversely their Lie weights occur in $\operatorname{Lie}K$, since their Lie inclusions are injective, and therefore their entire semigroup lies in that of $K$. This proves(c). No equality of the generated Lie algebra with $\operatorname{Lie}K$ is asserted, and no strictly definite weight assumption or finite generating set of $A$ was used.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let $T$ be a maximal torus. Then Chevalley's theorem holds: $R_u(G)=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B_u)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $R_u(G)\cdot T=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the intersections running over the finite set of Borel subgroups containing $T$. Consequently, for any torus $S$ in $G$ one has $R_u(C_G(S))=R_u(G)\cap C_G(S)$, and for a torus $S$ acting on $G$ one has $R_u(G^S)=R_u(G)^S$. In particular, if $G$ is reductive, then $C_G(S)=G^S$ is smooth, connected and reductive for every torus $S\subseteq G$, and $C_G(T)=T$ for every maximal torus $T$ of a reductive $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over $k$ equipped with an action of a split torus $T$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]), and let $\Psi=\Psi(G,T)$ be the set of weights of $T$ on $\mathfrak g$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). (a) If $A\subseteq X(T)$ is a subsemigroup, then there is a unique $T$-stable connected subgroup variety $H_A\subseteq G$ whose weight set is $A\cap\Psi$, so that $\operatorname{Lie}(H_A)=\bigoplus_{\chi\in A\cap\Psi}\mathfrak g_\chi$; every $T$-stable connected subgroup variety whose Lie algebra is contained in $\operatorname{Lie}(H_A)$ is contained in $H_A$. (b) If $A=(\alpha)$ is the cyclic semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of a nonzero weight $\alpha$, and $\lambda$ is a cocharacter of $T$ with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0$, then $H_{(\alpha)}=U_G(\lambda)$ is the concentrator of $e$ for the action of $\lambda$ on $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$, $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ$; it is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra the sum of the weight spaces of the rational multiples of $\alpha$, and every $T$-stable subgroup containing it in its Lie algebra contains it. (c) If $G$ is generated by $T$-stable connected subgroups $H_1,H_2$, then the generated subgroup is smooth and connected, and its weight semigroup is generated by those of $H_1$ and $H_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth algebraic group over $k$ and let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a cocharacter, acting on $G$ by $t\cdot g=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]] for the notation, [[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then $P_G(\lambda)=G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\})$, $Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ (the fibre of $g\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g$ over $e$) are algebraic subgroups of $G$, with $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ normal in $P_G(\lambda)$; over $k^{\mathrm a}$, $P_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ are the unique smooth subgroups whose geometric points are the $g$ with the indicated limits. If $G$ is smooth, then $P_G(\lambda),Z_G(\lambda),U_G(\lambda)$ are smooth; the multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism; $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is an open immersion; $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected and unipotent; and under the weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the $\mathbf G_m$-action one has $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}U_G(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$. If moreover $G$ is reductive, then $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)\cong Z_G(\lambda)$ is reductive and $R_u(P_G(\lambda))=U_G(\lambda)$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The adjoint representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a rational representation, so $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak t=\operatorname{Lie}(T)=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ and the **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_\alpha\neq0$ ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal subtorus of $\ker\alpha$, of codimension one in $T$, $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, the subgroup attached to the cyclic semigroup of positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ by [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]]; $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$ ([[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]). The **Weyl group** of the pair is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ ([[lem-fixed-loci-and-centralizers-of-torus-actions-are-connected]]). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the system of **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, with $-\Phi^+(B)$ the negative roots relative to $B$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]).

The Weyl group is a finite étale group scheme, being the quotient of the normalizer of the torus by the torus itself; it acts faithfully on $X(T)$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). The root groups $U_\alpha$ depend only on the root $\alpha$ and not on the auxiliary cocharacter used in their construction, because the cyclic semigroup $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic: it consists of the positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ that belong to the character lattice, and the subgroup $H_{(\alpha)}$ of [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]] is characterized by its weight semigroup. The positive system of a Borel subgroup determines and is determined by the Borel subgroup: two Borels containing $T$ yield the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne, Ch. 21), a fact used in the proof of the Weyl-group theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ of semisimple rank $1$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Then there exists a homomorphism $v:(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)\to(G,T)$ with central kernel, and every such homomorphism is a central isogeny from $\mathrm{SL}_2$ onto the derived group $G'$; any two differ by the inner automorphism defined by an element of $(N_{\mathrm{SL}_2}(T_2)/\mu_2)(k)$. Moreover $v$ maps $U^\pm$ isomorphically onto the root groups of $\Phi(G,T)$, and for either chosen root $\alpha$, if $T_1=(T\cap G')^\circ$ is the unique maximal torus of the derived group contained in $T$, then there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T_1)$ with $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. In particular the two root groups generate $G\prime$, which is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_2$ or $\mathrm{PGL}_2$; together with $T$ they generate $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field, $T_2$ the diagonal torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$ ([[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]], [[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]). Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-lie-algebra-of-a-group-scheme]]), and let $H,H_1,H_2$ be algebraic subgroups. (a) For a finite inverse system $(G_i)$ of algebraic groups, $\operatorname{Lie}(\varprojlim G_i)\cong\varprojlim\operatorname{Lie}(G_i)$; in particular $\operatorname{Lie}$ is left exact on exact sequences and $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\times_G H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\times_{\operatorname{Lie}(G)}\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$, so if $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ then $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\cap H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$ ([[lem-lie-algebra-tangent-space-and-functoriality]]). (b) If $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, $H$ is smooth and $G$ is connected, then $H=G$; if the Lie algebras of smooth subgroups $H_1,\dots,H_n$ generate $\mathfrak g$ as a Lie algebra and $G$ is connected, then the $H_i$ generate $G$. (c) If $H$ acts on $G$ by conjugation, then $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(H))=\mathfrak g^H$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(N_G(H)/H)=(\mathfrak g/\operatorname{Lie}(H))^H$; in particular $\dim C_G(H)\le\dim\mathfrak g^H$, with equality iff $C_G(H)$ is smooth.

A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha}\ker\alpha$, and a **base** is a subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the direct sum $\mathbb Z\alpha\oplus\ker\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition; the lattice form, not the Euclidean one, is what is attached to a split reductive group in [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]].

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $X$ be a smooth connected variety over $k$ with an action of $\mathbf G_m$ ([[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). (a) **Luna's theorem:** if the action is definite (all weights of the gradation of $\mathcal O_X$ are $\ge0$), then the fixed locus $X^{\mathbf G_m}$ is connected, the limit map $X\to X^{\mathbf G_m}$, $x\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}tx$, exists, and for every $x\in X^{\mathbf G_m}$ the canonical $\mathbf G_m$-equivariant morphism $X\to T_x^+(X)$ into the positive part of the tangent space at $x$ is an isomorphism of varieties; this applies in particular to $X=G$ and to representable homogeneous spaces $X=G/P$. (b) **Bialynicki-Birula:** if $X$ is smooth, connected and complete and $X^{\mathbf G_m}$ is finite and constant, then for each fixed point $x$ there is a unique smooth subscheme $X(x)$ with $X(x)(k^{\mathrm a})=\{y:\lim_{t\to0}ty=x\}$, the tangent space at $x$ is the contracting subspace, $X(x)$ is an affine space, and the underlying topological space of $X$ is the disjoint union of the locally closed subsets $X(x)$; there is a unique attracting fixed point $x^-$ with $X(x^-)$ open dense and a unique repelling fixed point $x^+$ with $X(x^+)=\{x^+\}$.

derivations.claim: The subtorus $T_\alpha$ has codimension one in $T$ and is central in $G_\alpha$. Thus the semisimple rank of the split reductive group $G_\alpha$ is at most one. It is nonzero because its Lie algebra contains the nonzero root space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$, whereas a reductive group of semisimple rank zero is a torus. Apply [F2]: the central cover of $G_\alpha\prime$ has the two standard root groups of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, with one-dimensional root spaces. The central torus of $G_\alpha$ contributes only zero weights, so $G_\alpha$ has exactly two nonzero weights, $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$. By [F1], the roots of $G$ restricting trivially to $T_\alpha$ are precisely the rational multiples of $\alpha$; hence those multiples are only $\pm\alpha$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$. This proves (a).

Choose the central cover $v:\mathrm{SL}_2\to G_\alpha\prime$ from [F2], taking its diagonal torus onto $T_1=(T\cap G_\alpha\prime)^\circ$. Its standard root groups map isomorphically onto $U_{\pm\alpha}$, giving (b), including the Lie algebras and the smooth $T$-stable subgroup containment criterion of [F1]. The element $v(n_\alpha)$ normalizes $T_1$ and centralizes the central torus of $G_\alpha$, hence normalizes $T=T_1Z(G_\alpha)^\circ$. The Weyl group therefore has the two standard rank-one elements. Choose the sign of the image under $v$ of the standard coroot so that its pairing with $\alpha$ is $2$. On $T_1$ conjugation by $v(n_\alpha)$ acts by inversion, and on the central torus it acts trivially. These two subtori generate $T$ up to finite intersection, so the rank-one reflection formula holds on $X(T)\otimes\mathbb Q$, and hence on $X(T)$: $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. This formula determines the pairing of $\alpha^\vee$ with every character, proving its uniqueness in $X_*(T)$. This proves (c).

For (d): each root space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ is contained in $\operatorname{Lie}(T\cdot U_\alpha)$, so $\operatorname{Lie}$ of the subgroup $H$ generated by $T$ and the $U_\alpha$ contains $\mathfrak t$ and every root space, i.e. all of $\mathfrak g$; since $H$ is smooth (a generated subgroup of a reductive group by smooth subgroups is smooth, by the same generation criterion [F2]) and $G$ is connected, $H=G$ by the Lie-generation criterion [F2]. For (e): (rd1) is (c), (rd2) is the invariance of $\Phi$ under the reflections induced by conjugation with $n_\alpha$ (which maps $U_\beta$ to $U_{s_\alpha\beta}$ and hence permutes the root spaces), and (rd3) holds because $W(G,T)$ is finite (it is a quotient of the normalizer of a maximal torus, finite over $k$); the reflection subgroup acts simply transitively on the Weyl chambers, while $W(G,T)$ acts faithfully and simply transitively on the Borel subgroups containing $T$. The Borel–chamber bijection identifies these two sets, so the reflection subgroup has the same order as $W(G,T)$ and equals it (Milne's Weyl identification theorem).

For (f), choose a cocharacter strictly positive on $\Phi^+$. Its conjugation contracts $U=B_u$ and each positive root group to the identity. For any ordering, multiplication $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to U$ is equivariant and its differential at the identity is the direct-sum isomorphism of the positive root spaces. The strictly contracting smooth affine comparison in [F3] therefore makes it a global variety isomorphism; this is the argument of [F4] and uses no commutativity of the root groups. If $H\subseteq U$ is smooth and $T$-stable, the root-group containment criterion puts precisely the root groups corresponding to the weights of $\operatorname{Lie}H$ in $H^\circ$. The same contracting argument makes their ordered product isomorphic to $H^\circ$. To prove $H=H^\circ$, order those groups first in the coordinates of $U$. Those coordinates decompose $H$ as $H^\circ$ times a finite residual locus whose points have only the omitted root coordinates. The connected torus acts trivially on this finite component set, so that residual locus is fixed by $T$. But $U^T=U\cap C_G(T)=U\cap T=1$. Thus $H$ is connected and is exactly the ordered product of its root groups, proving the asserted subgroup description.

Let $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ be the weights of such an $H$. The Chevalley formula in [F4] and uniqueness of ordered root coordinates show that if $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$, the root $i\alpha+j\beta$ must be in $\Psi$: the corresponding coordinate of the commutator is a nonzero polynomial in $x,y$ and cannot be an omitted coordinate of $H$. Conversely, for quasi-closed $\Psi$, take the coordinate subvariety $H=\prod_{\alpha\in\Psi}U_\alpha$ in the coordinates of $U$. Collecting products and inverses using [F4] creates only root coordinates still in $\Psi$, so $H$ is a closed $T$-stable subgroup. Its product coordinates make it smooth connected with precisely those weights. Ordinary root closure implies quasi-closure by the root-string combinatorics. If $\operatorname{char}k=0$ or $\operatorname{char}k=p>3$, every structure coefficient that occurs in [F4] remains nonzero; in particular a root sum of two members of $\Psi$ must remain in $\Psi$. Thus quasi-closure and ordinary root closure coincide in those characteristics. This proves the corrected criterion.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement quantifies over root sets that may be empty; step 4.1 treats the empty product as the identity subgroup and step 5.1 includes the empty quasi-closed set.
The Statement includes root-free reductive groups: they are tori, generated by T; step 3.1 and the empty-product case of step 4.1 give the expected trivial unipotent radical.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove the rank-one root subgroup, central cover and coroot assertions with the full torus retained.

The Statement uses smooth subgroups for the product/weight criterion; step 5.1 uses quasi-closure in characteristics2/3 and ordinary closure only in characteristic0 or p>3. Given uses the maximal kernel subtorus, avoiding nonreduced mu2 as a torus.

For Root subgroups of a split reductive group and the reduced root datum: The statement asserts an equivalence; the forward direction is proved in the first named direction of the proof, whose steps are mapped in the derivations.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a reductive algebraic group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]) and let $T$ be a maximal torus of $G$. Then: (a) $Z(G)\subseteq T$ for every maximal torus $T$, and $Z(G)$ is of multiplicative type ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]]); (b) $R(G)=Z(G)_t$ is the largest subtorus of $Z(G)$ (not the full possibly nonreduced neutral component), its formation commutes with every extension of the base field, and the quotient $G/R(G)$ is semisimple; (c) $G/Z(G)$ has trivial centre; (d) the semisimple rank of $G$ equals $\operatorname{rk}G-\dim Z(G)$; (e) with $G'$ the derived subgroup ([[def-derived-subgroup-and-solvable-algebraic-group]]), $Z(G)_t\cap G'$ is finite, $G=Z(G)_t\cdot G'$ and the multiplication map $Z(G)_t\times G'\to G$ is surjective with finite kernel, and $G'$ is semisimple; (f) $G$ is semisimple iff $R(G)=1$ iff $Z(G)$ is finite. The quotient $G/R(G)$ is the represented normal affine quotient ([[thm-nonaffine-affine-normal-group-quotient-affine]]); it is smooth and connected by [[lem-nonaffine-exact-group-sequence-affine-smooth-connected-properties]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let $T$ be a maximal torus. Then Chevalley's theorem holds: $R_u(G)=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B_u)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $R_u(G)\cdot T=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the intersections running over the finite set of Borel subgroups containing $T$. Consequently, for any torus $S$ in $G$ one has $R_u(C_G(S))=R_u(G)\cap C_G(S)$, and for a torus $S$ acting on $G$ one has $R_u(G^S)=R_u(G)^S$. In particular, if $G$ is reductive, then $G^S$ is smooth, connected and reductive for every torus action by group automorphisms, in particular $C_G(S)$ has these properties for every torus $S\subseteq G$, and $C_G(T)=T$ for every maximal torus $T$ of a reductive $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric and smooth-local suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group variety over $k$ equipped with an action by automorphisms of a split torus $T$, and let $\Psi=\Psi(G,T)\subseteq X(T)$ be the weights of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}G$. Then:

(a) For every subsemigroup $A\subseteq X(T)$, there is a unique $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety $H_A\subseteq G$ with
$$\operatorname{Lie}H_A=\bigoplus_{\chi\in A\cap\Psi}\mathfrak g_\chi.$$
Every $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety whose Lie algebra is contained in this subspace is contained in $H_A$. No finite generation, saturation, exclusion of $0$, or strictly definite cone condition is imposed on $A$.

(b) For a nonzero weight $\alpha$, let $(\alpha)$ be the semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ lying in $X(T)$, and let $\lambda$ be a cocharacter with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0$. Put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)_t$, the largest reduced subtorus of its kernel, and $G_\alpha=G^{T_\alpha}$, the fixed subgroup for the given external action. Then $H_{(\alpha)}=U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)$, the identity concentrator for this action on $G_\alpha$; it is smooth connected unipotent and $T$-stable, with Lie algebra the sum of the strictly positive rational-$\alpha$ weight spaces. Every $T$-stable **smooth** subgroup variety $H\subseteq G$ with $\operatorname{Lie}H\supseteq\operatorname{Lie}H_{(\alpha)}$ contains $H_{(\alpha)}$. The smoothness qualification is necessary: $\alpha_p\subseteq\mathbf G_a$ with the scaling torus has the same Lie algebra as $\mathbf G_a$, but does not contain that positive-weight subgroup.

(c) The closed subgroup generated by two $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup varieties $H_1,H_2$ is smooth connected, and its weight semigroup is generated by their weight semigroups. Here a weight semigroup means the semigroup of nonempty finite sums of Lie weights; the empty weight set generates the empty semigroup. If $H_1,H_2$ generate $G$, this identifies the weight semigroup of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth algebraic group over $k$ and let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a cocharacter, acting on $G$ by $t\cdot g=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]] for the notation, [[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then $P_G(\lambda)=G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\})$, $Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ (the fibre of $g\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g$ over $e$) are algebraic subgroups of $G$, with $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ normal in $P_G(\lambda)$; over $k^{\mathrm a}$, $P_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ are the unique smooth subgroups whose geometric points are the $g$ with the indicated limits. Then $P_G(\lambda),Z_G(\lambda),U_G(\lambda)$ are smooth; the multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism; $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is an open immersion; $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected and unipotent; and under the weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the $\mathbf G_m$-action one has $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}U_G(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$. If moreover $G$ is reductive, then $P_G(\lambda)/U_G(\lambda)\cong Z_G(\lambda)$ is reductive and $R_u(P_G(\lambda))=U_G(\lambda)$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ for which the adjoint weight space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ in $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}G$ is nonzero. The adjoint action is rational, and the weight decomposition
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$$
is the choice-free decomposition into character eigenspaces ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). This nonzero-weight definition uses no choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the following supplemental structural facts and subgroup constructions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The reductive centralizer identity $C_G(T)=T$ and Lie fixed-point equality give $\mathfrak g_0=\operatorname{Lie}T=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ ([[thm-chevalley-centralizer-radical-and-reductive-centralizers]], [[lem-lie-functor-exactness-fixed-points-and-generation]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$, put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)_t=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal reduced subtorus of its kernel, of codimension one in $T$, and $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$. The **root group** is $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, attached to the semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ in $X(T)$; it is smooth connected unipotent and $T$-stable with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$. Its identity-concentrator construction takes place in $G_\alpha$, not in all of $G$ ([[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]], [[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]).

The **Weyl group** is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$. Under the stated AC premise it is a finite étale group scheme and acts faithfully on $X(T)$ (Milne21.1 and21.12). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}B\}$ and negative roots $-\Phi^+(B)$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]], [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). Root groups are independent of the auxiliary cocharacter because $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic and its smooth connected subgroup is characterized by its specified Lie weight subspace. Two Borels containing $T$ give the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne21.23 and21.35). These structural facts inherit the explicit AC premise; the definition of a root as a nonzero adjoint character above remains choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ of semisimple rank $1$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Then there exists a homomorphism $v:(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)\to(G,T)$ with central kernel, and every such homomorphism is a central isogeny from $\mathrm{SL}_2$ onto the derived group $G'$; any two differ by the inner automorphism defined by an element of $(N_{\mathrm{SL}_2}(T_2)/\mu_2)(k)$. Moreover $v$ maps $U^\pm$ isomorphically onto the root groups of $\Phi(G,T)$, and for either chosen root $\alpha$, if $T_1=(T\cap G')_t$ is the unique maximal torus of the derived group contained in $T$, then there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T_1)$ with $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. In particular the two root groups generate $G\prime$, which is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_2$ or $\mathrm{PGL}_2$; together with $T$ they generate $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field, $T_2$ the diagonal torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$ ([[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]], [[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]). Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric and smooth-local suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group variety over $k$ equipped with an action by automorphisms of a split torus $T$, and let $\Psi=\Psi(G,T)\subseteq X(T)$ be the weights of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}G$. Then:

(a) For every subsemigroup $A\subseteq X(T)$, there is a unique $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety $H_A\subseteq G$ with
$$\operatorname{Lie}H_A=\bigoplus_{\chi\in A\cap\Psi}\mathfrak g_\chi.$$
Every $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup variety whose Lie algebra is contained in this subspace is contained in $H_A$. No finite generation, saturation, exclusion of $0$, or strictly definite cone condition is imposed on $A$.

(b) For a nonzero weight $\alpha$, let $(\alpha)$ be the semigroup of strictly positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ lying in $X(T)$, and let $\lambda$ be a cocharacter with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0$. Put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)_t$, the largest reduced subtorus of its kernel, and $G_\alpha=G^{T_\alpha}$, the fixed subgroup for the given external action. Then $H_{(\alpha)}=U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)$, the identity concentrator for this action on $G_\alpha$; it is smooth connected unipotent and $T$-stable, with Lie algebra the sum of the strictly positive rational-$\alpha$ weight spaces. Every $T$-stable **smooth** subgroup variety $H\subseteq G$ with $\operatorname{Lie}H\supseteq\operatorname{Lie}H_{(\alpha)}$ contains $H_{(\alpha)}$. The smoothness qualification is necessary: $\alpha_p\subseteq\mathbf G_a$ with the scaling torus has the same Lie algebra as $\mathbf G_a$, but does not contain that positive-weight subgroup.

(c) The closed subgroup generated by two $T$-stable smooth connected subgroup varieties $H_1,H_2$ is smooth connected, and its weight semigroup is generated by their weight semigroups. Here a weight semigroup means the semigroup of nonempty finite sums of Lie weights; the empty weight set generates the empty semigroup. If $H_1,H_2$ generate $G$, this identifies the weight semigroup of $G$.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-lie-algebra-of-a-group-scheme]]), and let $H,H_1,H_2$ be algebraic subgroups. (a) For a finite inverse system $(G_i)$ of algebraic groups, $\operatorname{Lie}(\varprojlim G_i)\cong\varprojlim\operatorname{Lie}(G_i)$; in particular $\operatorname{Lie}$ is left exact on exact sequences and $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\times_G H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\times_{\operatorname{Lie}(G)}\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$, so if $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ then $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\cap H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$ ([[lem-lie-algebra-tangent-space-and-functoriality]]). (b) If $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, $H$ is smooth and $G$ is connected, then $H=G$; if the Lie algebras of smooth subgroups $H_1,\dots,H_n$ generate $\mathfrak g$ as a Lie algebra and $G$ is connected, then the $H_i$ generate $G$. (c) If $H$ acts on $G$ by conjugation, then $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(H))=\mathfrak g^H$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(N_G(H))/\operatorname{Lie}(H)=(\mathfrak g/\operatorname{Lie}(H))^H$; in particular $\dim C_G(H)\le\dim\mathfrak g^H$, with equality iff $C_G(H)$ is smooth.

A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition; the lattice form, not the Euclidean one, is what is attached to a split reductive group in [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]].

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $X$ be a smooth geometrically connected variety over $k$ with an action of $\mathbf G_m$.

(a) **Definite affine actions and Luna maps.** Suppose $X$ is affine and its coordinate ring is nonnegatively graded, $A=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}A_n$. Then the fixed locus $F=X^{\mathbf G_m}=\operatorname{Spec}A_0$ is smooth and connected, and the limit retraction $p:X\to F$ realizes $X$ as the vector bundle associated with the finite projective $A_0$-module $I/I^2$, where $I=\bigoplus_{n>0}A_n$. This isomorphism depends on choices of homogeneous lifts. If $x\in F(k)$ and every tangent weight at $x$ is strictly positive, then $F=\{x\}$ and every Luna map $X\to T_xX=T_x^+X$ obtained from a homogeneous complement of $\mathfrak m_x^2$ in $\mathfrak m_x$ is an equivariant isomorphism. More generally, an equivariant morphism between smooth geometrically connected affine varieties with strictly positive tangent weights at a fixed rational point is an isomorphism if its differential there is an isomorphism. No canonical choice of Luna map is asserted.

(b) **Bialynicki-Birula decomposition.** Suppose the action is locally affine, $X$ is complete and the fixed scheme is finite and constant. For each fixed point $x$ the attracting scheme $X(x)$ is smooth, locally closed, and equivariantly isomorphic by a Luna map to the affine space $T_x^+X$. Its geometric points are precisely the $y$ with $\lim_{t\to0}ty=x$, and $T_xX(x)=T_x^+X$. The topological space of $X$ is the disjoint union of these cells. There is a unique attracting point $x^-$ with $X(x^-)$ open dense and a unique repelling point $x^+$ with $X(x^+)=\{x^+\}$. These conclusions apply to smooth homogeneous spaces satisfying the stated action hypotheses; affineness or strict contraction is not automatic for an arbitrary $G/P$.

derivations.claim: The subtorus $T_\alpha$ has codimension one in $T$ and is central in $G_\alpha$. Thus the semisimple rank of the split reductive group $G_\alpha$ is at most one. It is nonzero because its Lie algebra contains the nonzero root space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$, whereas a reductive group of semisimple rank zero is a torus. Apply [F2]: the central cover of $G_\alpha\prime$ has the two standard root groups of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, with one-dimensional root spaces. The central torus $Z(G_\alpha)_t$ contributes only zero weights, by the exact central-torus product clause of [F1], so $G_\alpha$ has exactly two nonzero weights, $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$. By [F1], the roots of $G$ restricting trivially to $T_\alpha$ are precisely the rational multiples of $\alpha$; hence those multiples are only $\pm\alpha$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$. This proves (a).

Choose the central cover $v:\mathrm{SL}_2\to G_\alpha\prime$ from [F2], taking its diagonal torus onto $T_1=(T\cap G_\alpha\prime)_t$. Its standard root groups map isomorphically onto $U_{\pm\alpha}$, giving (b), including the Lie algebras and the smooth $T$-stable subgroup containment criterion of [F1]. The element $v(n_\alpha)$ normalizes $T_1$ and centralizes the central torus of $G_\alpha$, hence normalizes $T=T_1Z(G_\alpha)_t$. The Weyl group therefore has the two standard rank-one elements. Choose the sign of the image under $v$ of the standard coroot so that its pairing with $\alpha$ is $2$. On $T_1$ conjugation by $v(n_\alpha)$ acts by inversion, and on the central torus it acts trivially. These two subtori generate $T$ up to finite intersection, so the rank-one reflection formula holds on $X(T)\otimes\mathbb Q$, and hence on $X(T)$: $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. This formula determines the pairing of $\alpha^\vee$ with every character, proving its uniqueness in $X_*(T)$. This proves (c).

For (d): each root space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ is contained in $\operatorname{Lie}(T\cdot U_\alpha)$, so $\operatorname{Lie}$ of the subgroup $H$ generated by $T$ and the $U_\alpha$ contains $\mathfrak t$ and every root space, i.e. all of $\mathfrak g$; since $H$ is smooth (a generated subgroup of a reductive group by smooth subgroups is smooth, by the same generation criterion [F2]) and $G$ is connected, $H=G$ by the Lie-generation criterion [F2]. For (e): (rd1) is (c), (rd2) follows on roots from conjugation by $n_\alpha$, which sends $U_\beta$ to $U_{s_\alpha\beta}$; the uniqueness characterization of each coroot in(c) also sends $\beta^\vee$ to $(s_\alpha\beta)^\vee$ under the dual conjugation action, giving the required coroot-reflection invariance, and (rd3) holds because $W(G,T)$ is finite (it is a quotient of the normalizer of a maximal torus, finite over $k$); the reflection subgroup acts simply transitively on the Weyl chambers, while $W(G,T)$ acts faithfully and simply transitively on the Borel subgroups containing $T$. The Borel–chamber bijection identifies these two sets, so the reflection subgroup has the same order as $W(G,T)$ and equals it (Milne's Weyl identification theorem).

For (f), choose a cocharacter strictly positive on $\Phi^+$. Its conjugation contracts $U=B_u$ and each positive root group to the identity. For any ordering, multiplication $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to U$ is equivariant and its differential at the identity is the direct-sum isomorphism of the positive root spaces. The strictly contracting smooth affine comparison in [F3] therefore makes it a global variety isomorphism; this is the argument of [F4] and uses no commutativity of the root groups. If $H\subseteq U$ is smooth and $T$-stable, the root-group containment criterion puts precisely the root groups corresponding to the weights of $\operatorname{Lie}H$ in $H^\circ$. The same contracting argument makes their ordered product isomorphic to $H^\circ$. To prove $H=H^\circ$, order those groups first in the coordinates of $U$. Those coordinates decompose $H$ as $H^\circ$ times a finite residual locus whose points have only the omitted root coordinates. The connected torus acts trivially on this finite component set, so that residual locus is fixed by $T$. But $U^T=U\cap C_G(T)=U\cap T=1$. Thus $H$ is connected and is exactly the ordered product of its root groups, proving the asserted subgroup description.

Let $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ be the weights of such an $H$. The Chevalley formula in [F4] and uniqueness of ordered root coordinates show that if $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$, the root $i\alpha+j\beta$ must be in $\Psi$: the corresponding coordinate of the commutator is a nonzero polynomial in $x,y$ and cannot be an omitted coordinate of $H$. Conversely, for quasi-closed $\Psi$, take the coordinate subvariety $H=\prod_{\alpha\in\Psi}U_\alpha$ in the coordinates of $U$. Collecting products and inverses using [F4] creates only root coordinates still in $\Psi$, so $H$ is a closed $T$-stable subgroup. Its product coordinates make it smooth connected with precisely those weights. Ordinary root closure implies quasi-closure by the root-string combinatorics. If $\operatorname{char}k=0$ or $\operatorname{char}k=p>3$, every structure coefficient that occurs in [F4] remains nonzero; in particular a root sum of two members of $\Psi$ must remain in $\Psi$. Thus quasi-closure and ordinary root closure coincide in those characteristics. This proves the corrected criterion.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The adjoint representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a rational representation, so $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak t=\operatorname{Lie}(T)=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ and the **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_\alpha\neq0$ ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal subtorus of $\ker\alpha$, of codimension one in $T$, $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, the subgroup attached to the cyclic semigroup of positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ by [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]]; $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$ ([[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]). The **Weyl group** of the pair is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ ([[lem-fixed-loci-and-centralizers-of-torus-actions-are-connected]]). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the system of **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, with $-\Phi^+(B)$ the negative roots relative to $B$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]).

The Weyl group is a finite étale group scheme, being the quotient of the normalizer of the torus by the torus itself; it acts faithfully on $X(T)$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). The root groups $U_\alpha$ depend only on the root $\alpha$ and not on the auxiliary cocharacter used in their construction, because the cyclic semigroup $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic: it consists of the positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ that belong to the character lattice, and the subgroup $H_{(\alpha)}$ of [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]] is characterized by its weight semigroup. The positive system of a Borel subgroup determines and is determined by the Borel subgroup: two Borels containing $T$ yield the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne, Ch. 21), a fact used in the proof of the Weyl-group theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and let $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$. Every Borel subgroup $B$ of $G$ containing $T$ contains exactly one of the two root groups $U_\alpha$, $U_{-\alpha}$, and $B\cap G_\alpha$ is a Borel subgroup of $G_\alpha$; exactly two Borel subgroups of $G_\alpha$ contain $T$, namely $U_\alpha T$ and $U_{-\alpha}T$. Moreover, for a cocharacter $\lambda$ of $T$ that is regular ($\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\neq0$ for all roots $\alpha$), $P_G(\lambda)$ is the unique Borel subgroup of $G$ containing $T$ with $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak t\oplus\bigoplus_{\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, and $\lambda\mapsto P_G(\lambda)$ induces a bijection from the set of Weyl chambers onto the set of Borel subgroups containing $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over $k$. (a) A torus $T\subseteq G$ is maximal iff $T_{k'}$ is maximal in $G_{k'}$ for every field extension $k'/k$; equivalently iff $C_G(T)/T$ contains no nontrivial torus. (b) There is a maximal torus of $G_{k^{\mathrm a}}$ defined over $k$. (c) If $G$ is reductive, then a torus $T\subseteq G$ is maximal iff $C_G(T)=T$. (d) If $N\subseteq G$ is a connected normal subgroup variety and $T$ a maximal torus of $G$, then $(T\cap N)^\circ$ is a maximal torus of $N$, and every maximal torus of $N$ arises this way. (e) If $G=G_1\cdots G_n$ is an almost-direct product of connected subgroup varieties, then every maximal torus $T$ of $G$ is an almost-direct product $T=(T\cap G_1)^\circ\cdots(T\cap G_n)^\circ$. (f) Any two maximal tori of $G$ become conjugate over some finite separable extension of $k$; in particular they are conjugate over a separably closed field.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a connected affine group variety over $k$, i.e. a smooth connected affine algebraic group of finite type over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then: (a) for every Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ the quotient $G/B$ is complete; (b) any two Borel subgroups of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (c) any two maximal tori of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (d) any two Borel pairs are conjugate. The hypotheses connected and smooth, and the algebraic closedness of $k$, are essential; the statements are not claimed over general fields or for nonsmooth groups.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The adjoint representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a rational representation, so $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak t=\operatorname{Lie}(T)=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ and the **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_\alpha\neq0$ ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal subtorus of $\ker\alpha$, of codimension one in $T$, $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, the subgroup attached to the cyclic semigroup of positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ by [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]]; $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$ ([[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]). The **Weyl group** of the pair is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ ([[lem-fixed-loci-and-centralizers-of-torus-actions-are-connected]]). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the system of **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, with $-\Phi^+(B)$ the negative roots relative to $B$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]).

The Weyl group is a finite étale group scheme, being the quotient of the normalizer of the torus by the torus itself; it acts faithfully on $X(T)$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). The root groups $U_\alpha$ depend only on the root $\alpha$ and not on the auxiliary cocharacter used in their construction, because the cyclic semigroup $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic: it consists of the positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ that belong to the character lattice, and the subgroup $H_{(\alpha)}$ of [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]] is characterized by its weight semigroup. The positive system of a Borel subgroup determines and is determined by the Borel subgroup: two Borels containing $T$ yield the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne, Ch. 21), a fact used in the proof of the Weyl-group theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Over an arbitrary field $k$, $G\mapsto X^*(G)$ is a contravariant equivalence between finite-type group schemes of multiplicative type over $k$ and finitely generated abelian groups with continuous $\Gamma_k$-action. Its inverse sends $M$ to the group with coordinate algebra $(k_s[M])^{\Gamma_k}$ for the action $\sigma(c e_m)=\sigma(c)e_{\sigma m}$. In particular, naturally,
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-groups}}(G,H)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma_k}(X^*(H),X^*(G)).$$
No smoothness, connectedness, perfection, or characteristic-zero hypothesis is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a connected group variety over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let $T$ be a maximal torus. Then Chevalley's theorem holds: $R_u(G)=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B_u)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $R_u(G)\cdot T=(\bigcap_{B\supseteq T}B)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the intersections running over the finite set of Borel subgroups containing $T$. Consequently, for any torus $S$ in $G$ one has $R_u(C_G(S))=R_u(G)\cap C_G(S)$, and for a torus $S$ acting on $G$ one has $R_u(G^S)=R_u(G)^S$. In particular, if $G$ is reductive, then $C_G(S)=G^S$ is smooth, connected and reductive for every torus $S\subseteq G$, and $C_G(T)=T$ for every maximal torus $T$ of a reductive $G$.
