derivations.claim: Since $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ by (rd1), every $\alpha\in\Phi$ is nonzero, and $\Phi$ is finite and spans $V_0$ by construction; each $s_\alpha$ preserves $V_0$, acts on $x\in V_0$ by $x\mapsto x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$, fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$ and sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$. Restricting the coroots to $V_0$ gives functionals $\bar\alpha^\vee$ with $\langle\Phi,\bar\alpha^\vee\rangle\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$, so $(V_0,\Phi)$ satisfies the root-system axioms with coroots $\bar\alpha^\vee$; reducedness of the root datum is exactly the reducedness of this root system. Since $W(R)$ is finite by (rd3) and acts on the finite-dimensional real vector space $V_0\otimes\mathbb R$, averaging an arbitrary inner product over $W(R)$ produces an invariant inner product. For an invariant inner product the relation $\langle x,\bar\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(x,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ holds for all $x$, and the right side is independent of the choice of invariant inner product; hence $s_\alpha|_{V_0}$ is the orthogonal reflection with vector $\alpha$ of the Euclidean theory, and the image of $W(R)$ in $\operatorname{GL}(V_0)$ is precisely the Weyl group $W(\Phi)$ of the reduced crystallographic root system $(V_0,\Phi)$ in the sense of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]].

The natural map $W(R)\to W(\Phi)$ is surjective because the reflections generating the latter are restrictions of the generators of $W(R)$. For injectivity let $w$ restrict to the identity on $V_0$. Each reflection acts as the identity on $V/V_0$, where $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$, since its difference from the identity has image in the root line. Consequently $D=w-1$ sends $V$ into $V_0$ and vanishes on $V_0$, so $D^2=0$. The finite group $W(R)$ gives $w^m=1$ for some positive integer $m$; the binomial identity $(1+D)^m=1+mD$ then forces $D=0$ over $\mathbb Q$. Thus $w=1$ and $W(R)\cong W(\Phi)$. This also transfers finiteness, faithful action on the roots, and generation by the simple reflections of any base.

By the identification $W(R)=W(\Phi)$ of step 2.1, [F2] transfers verbatim: the simple roots of a base $\Delta$ form a basis, every root is an integral combination of $\Delta$ with coefficients of one sign, the Weyl chambers are the connected components of the complement of the hyperplanes $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on them. Moreover the sign conditions defining positive systems and the indecomposability defining simple roots are the same in the two languages, so bases, positive systems and chambers correspond bijectively, and simple transitivity on chambers is equivalent to simple transitivity on bases.

By [F3] applied to $(V_0,\Phi)$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w$ the inversion number $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length in simple reflections. Further $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$, because length is the minimum word length and $w^{-1}=s_{i_m}\cdots s_{i_1}$ whenever $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_m}$ is minimal. Finally $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$. For $\alpha\in\Phi^+$ put $\beta=-w_0^{-1}\alpha\in\Phi^+$; this is a bijection of $\Phi^+$. The condition $\alpha\in w_0w(\Phi^-)$ says $w^{-1}w_0^{-1}\alpha\in\Phi^-$, equivalently $w^{-1}\beta\in\Phi^+$. These are precisely the complement of the $n(w)$ positive roots whose image under $w^{-1}$ is negative. Therefore the required count is $|\Phi^+|-n(w)$. If the root datum is semisimple, then $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$, so $\mathbb Q\Phi=X\otimes\mathbb Q=V$ and $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense by step 1.1; conversely if $\Phi$ spans $X\otimes\mathbb Q$ then the finitely generated subgroup $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has full rank, hence finite index, in $X$, so the root datum is semisimple.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ with root datum $(X,\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-lie-algebra-of-a-group-scheme]]), and let $H,H_1,H_2$ be algebraic subgroups. (a) For a finite inverse system $(G_i)$ of algebraic groups, $\operatorname{Lie}(\varprojlim G_i)\cong\varprojlim\operatorname{Lie}(G_i)$; in particular $\operatorname{Lie}$ is left exact on exact sequences and $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\times_G H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\times_{\operatorname{Lie}(G)}\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$, so if $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ then $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\cap H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$ ([[lem-lie-algebra-tangent-space-and-functoriality]]). (b) If $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, $H$ is smooth and $G$ is connected, then $H=G$; if the Lie algebras of smooth subgroups $H_1,\dots,H_n$ generate $\mathfrak g$ as a Lie algebra and $G$ is connected, then the $H_i$ generate $G$. (c) If $H$ acts on $G$ by conjugation, then $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(H))=\mathfrak g^H$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(N_G(H)/H)=(\mathfrak g/\operatorname{Lie}(H))^H$; in particular $\dim C_G(H)\le\dim\mathfrak g^H$, with equality iff $C_G(H)$ is smooth.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). The adjoint representation of $T$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is a rational representation, so $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak t=\operatorname{Lie}(T)=C_{\mathfrak g}(T)$ and the **roots** $\Phi(G,T)$ are the nontrivial characters $\alpha\in X(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_\alpha\neq0$ ([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]], [[lem-adjoint-representation-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put $T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}$, the maximal subtorus of $\ker\alpha$, of codimension one in $T$, $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and $U_\alpha=H_{(\alpha)}\subseteq G_\alpha$, the subgroup attached to the cyclic semigroup of positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ by [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]]; $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable and connected with Lie algebra $\bigoplus_{\beta\in(\alpha)\cap\Phi}\mathfrak g_\beta$ ([[thm-cocharacter-limit-subgroups]]). The **Weyl group** of the pair is $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ ([[lem-fixed-loci-and-centralizers-of-torus-actions-are-connected]]). A Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ determines the system of **positive roots** $\Phi^+(B)=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\mathfrak g_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(B)\}$, with $-\Phi^+(B)$ the negative roots relative to $B$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]]).

The Weyl group is a finite étale group scheme, being the quotient of the normalizer of the torus by the torus itself; it acts faithfully on $X(T)$ ([[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). The root groups $U_\alpha$ depend only on the root $\alpha$ and not on the auxiliary cocharacter used in their construction, because the cyclic semigroup $(\alpha)$ is intrinsic: it consists of the positive rational multiples of $\alpha$ that belong to the character lattice, and the subgroup $H_{(\alpha)}$ of [[thm-weight-subgroups-of-a-torus-action]] is characterized by its weight semigroup. The positive system of a Borel subgroup determines and is determined by the Borel subgroup: two Borels containing $T$ yield the same positive roots exactly when they are equal (Milne, Ch. 21), a fact used in the proof of the Weyl-group theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $H$ be the subgroup generated by $T$ and the $G_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$. Each $G_\alpha$ contains its two root groups and a representative of $s_\alpha$, by the rank-one results in [F1]. As the simple reflections generate $W$, products of these representatives in $H$ represent every $w\in W$. Conjugation by them and $W\cdot\Delta=\Phi$ show that $H$ contains every root group. It therefore equals $G$ by [F1]. Each $G_\alpha$ is generated by $T$ and its two root groups, so this also proves generation by $T$ and the simple positive and negative root groups. If $G$ is semisimple, let $K$ be generated by all root groups. The standard $\mathrm{SL}_2$ root-group generation in each rank-one derived subgroup puts every coroot image in $K$. The coroots span $X_*(T)\otimes\mathbb Q$ for semisimple $G$, so these images generate $T$. Thus $K=G$. If $\Delta$ is empty, $G=T$ and the first assertion still holds; a semisimple group with empty root system is trivial.

The subgroups $U_w$ and $U^w$ are smooth connected $T$-stable by [F2], being generated by root groups with weight sets $\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^+$ and $\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-$ respectively; these two subsets of $\Phi^+$ are disjoint and their union is $\Phi^+$ (a positive root is either in $w\Phi^+$ or in $w\Phi^-$), and each is ordinarily closed: a positive root sum of members remains positive and its inverse image under $w$ retains the same positive or negative sign. Ordinary closure is sufficient by [F2], so each is the weight set of a smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $U$ and the product decomposition of $U$ from [F2] gives a $T$-equivariant isomorphism $U_w\times U^w\to U$. The membership criterion for root groups follows because $U_\alpha\subseteq U_w$ iff the weight $\alpha$ belongs to the weight set of $U_w$ (uniqueness of the smooth subgroup with a given weight semigroup in [F2]). This proves (b).

Scheme-theoretically, the stabilizer of $n_wB$ in $U$ is $U\cap n_wBn_w^{-1}$. The root-coordinate intersection result for smooth $T$-stable subgroups gives it precisely the root groups indexed by $\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^+$, hence it is $U_w$; this is the stabilizer computation in the cited Milne orbit propositions. Order the complementary root groups first in [F2]. The resulting multiplication isomorphism $U^w\times U_w\to U$ identifies the fppf quotient $U/U_w$ with $U^w$, because right multiplication by $U_w$ changes only the second factor. The homogeneous orbit map identifies $U/U_w$ with $Un_wB/B$, proving the claimed orbit isomorphism without relying on a merely pointwise bijection. Its dimension is $\dim U^w=|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|=n(w)$ by [F1] and root-datum combinatorics.

Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-lie-algebra-of-a-group-scheme]]), and let $H,H_1,H_2$ be algebraic subgroups. (a) For a finite inverse system $(G_i)$ of algebraic groups, $\operatorname{Lie}(\varprojlim G_i)\cong\varprojlim\operatorname{Lie}(G_i)$; in particular $\operatorname{Lie}$ is left exact on exact sequences and $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\times_G H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\times_{\operatorname{Lie}(G)}\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$, so if $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ then $\operatorname{Lie}(H_1\cap H_2)=\operatorname{Lie}(H_1)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(H_2)$ ([[lem-lie-algebra-tangent-space-and-functoriality]]). (b) If $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, $H$ is smooth and $G$ is connected, then $H=G$; if the Lie algebras of smooth subgroups $H_1,\dots,H_n$ generate $\mathfrak g$ as a Lie algebra and $G$ is connected, then the $H_i$ generate $G$. (c) If $H$ acts on $G$ by conjugation, then $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(H))=\mathfrak g^H$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(N_G(H))/\operatorname{Lie}(H)=(\mathfrak g/\operatorname{Lie}(H))^H$; in particular $\dim C_G(H)\le\dim\mathfrak g^H$, with equality iff $C_G(H)$ is smooth.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the geometric suppliers. Let $G$ be a smooth algebraic group over $k$ and let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a cocharacter, acting on $G$ by $t\cdot g=\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]] for the notation, [[def-limit-of-a-gm-orbit-and-concentrator-subscheme]]). Then $P_G(\lambda)=G(\{g:\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g\text{ exists}\})$, $Z_G(\lambda)=C_G(\lambda(\mathbf G_m))$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ (the fibre of $g\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot g$ over $e$) are algebraic subgroups of $G$, with $P_G(\lambda)\cap P_G(-\lambda)=Z_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ normal in $P_G(\lambda)$; over $k^{\mathrm a}$, $P_G(\lambda)$ and $U_G(\lambda)$ are the unique smooth subgroups whose geometric points are the $g$ with the indicated limits. Then $P_G(\lambda),Z_G(\lambda),U_G(\lambda)$ are smooth; the multiplication map $U_G(\lambda)\rtimes Z_G(\lambda)\to P_G(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism; $U_G(-\lambda)\times P_G(\lambda)\to G$ is an open immersion; $U_G(\lambda)$ is connected and unipotent; and under the weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the $\mathbf G_m$-action one has $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}U_G(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}P_G(\lambda)=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$. derivations.claim: Let $H$ be the subgroup generated by $T$ and the $G_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$. Each $G_\alpha$ contains its two root groups and a representative of $s_\alpha$, by the rank-one results in [F1]. As the simple reflections generate $W$, products of these representatives in $H$ represent every $w\in W$. Conjugation by them and $W\cdot\Delta=\Phi$ show that $H$ contains every root group. It therefore equals $G$ by [F1]. Each $G_\alpha$ is generated by $T$ and its two root groups, so this also proves generation by $T$ and the simple positive and negative root groups. If $G$ is semisimple, let $K$ be generated by all root groups. The standard $\mathrm{SL}_2$ root-group generation in each rank-one derived subgroup puts every coroot image in $K$. The coroots span $X_*(T)\otimes\mathbb Q$ for semisimple $G$, so these images generate $T$. Thus $K=G$. If $\Delta$ is empty, $G=T$ and the first assertion still holds; a semisimple group with empty root system is trivial.

The subgroups $U_w$ and $U^w$ are smooth connected $T$-stable by [F2], being generated by root groups with weight sets $\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^+$ and $\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-$ respectively; these two subsets of $\Phi^+$ are disjoint and their union is $\Phi^+$ (a positive root is either in $w\Phi^+$ or in $w\Phi^-$), and each is ordinarily closed: a positive root sum of members remains positive and its inverse image under $w$ retains the same positive or negative sign. Ordinary closure is sufficient by [F2], so each is the weight set of a smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $U$ and the product decomposition of $U$ from [F2] gives a $T$-equivariant isomorphism $U_w\times U^w\to U$. The membership criterion for root groups follows because $U_\alpha\subseteq U_w$ iff the weight $\alpha$ belongs to the weight set of $U_w$ (uniqueness of the smooth subgroup with a given weight semigroup in [F2]). This proves (b).

The stabilizer of $n_wB$ in $U$ is $K=U\cap n_wBn_w^{-1}$. Work geometrically and take $K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ$, which is smooth connected over the algebraically closed field. citations.quote:
Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Its **root datum** is the quadruple
$$R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\Phi^\vee(G,T)),$$
where the character and cocharacter lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], the roots are the nonzero adjoint characters, and $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ consists of the associated coroots. Its **rank** is $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}X(T)=\dim T$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, its base $\Delta(B)$ consists of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots; the pair gives the based root datum $(R(G,T),\Delta(B))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the root-group, Weyl and centre suppliers for the following structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). By [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]] and [[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], the quadruple $R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\{\alpha^\vee\})$ is a reduced root datum in the sense of [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]: the lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], $\Phi(G,T)$ is the root system, $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ is the coroot bijection with $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$, and $W(R(G,T))$ is canonically $W(G,T)$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, the base $\Delta=\Delta(B)$ is the set of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots. The isomorphism class of $R(G,T)$ is independent of the choice of split Borel pair: if $(B',T')=g(B,T)g^{-1}$ for $g\in G(k)$, then conjugation by $g$ induces an isomorphism $R(G,T)\to R(G,T')$ independent of the choice of $g$, so $R(G,T)$ is well defined up to a unique isomorphism. Two remarks on the conventions. First, the base $\Delta(B)$ consists of the roots of the positive system that are indecomposable; by [[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]] it is indeed a base in the sense of the abstract definition, and $\Phi^+(B)$ is recovered as the nonnegative integral combinations of $\Delta(B)$. Second, the independence statement is a genuine well-definedness statement supplied by the named theorems: conjugation by an element $g$ with $gBg^{-1}=B'$ and $gTg^{-1}=T'$ induces a bijection of root systems and coroots, and two such elements differ by an element of $N_G(T)(k)$ whose induced action on $X(T)$ is trivial precisely when it lies in $T(k)$, so the induced isomorphism of root data is unique ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]]). This uniqueness is what allows the root datum to be written without choosing a Borel pair.

Then: (a) the double cosets $Bn_wB$ depend only on $w$, are smooth locally closed subvarieties of $G$, and $G$ is their disjoint union, $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}Bn_wB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}U_wn_wB$; (b) for every $w$ the multiplication map $U_w\times B\to Bn_wB$ is an isomorphism, and $G/B=\bigsqcup_wY(w)$ with $Y(w)=UwB/B\cong\mathbf A^{n(w)}$ an affine space of dimension $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|$; (c) the **big cell** $B^-B=U^-TB$ (with $B^-$ the opposite Borel, $B^-\cap B=T$ and $U^-=B^-_u$) is open and dense in $G$, the multiplication map $U^-\times T\times U\to G$ is an open immersion, and the big cell is the unique cell $Bn_{w_0}B$ of maximal dimension $|\Phi^+|$; (d) on $k$-points, $G(k)=\bigsqcup_wB(k)wB(k)$ is the Bruhat decomposition attached to the Tits system of [[lem-simple-reflection-double-coset-rule]], and the $G(k)$-orbits on $G/B\times G/B$ are in bijection with the $B(k)$-double cosets of $G(k)$, hence indexed by $W$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Let $k$ be a field, $T_2$ the diagonal torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$ ([[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]], [[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]). Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Its **root datum** is the quadruple
$$R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\Phi^\vee(G,T)),$$
where the character and cocharacter lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], the roots are the nonzero adjoint characters, and $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ consists of the associated coroots. Its **rank** is $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}X(T)=\dim T$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, its base $\Delta(B)$ consists of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots; the pair gives the based root datum $(R(G,T),\Delta(B))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the root-group, Weyl and centre suppliers for the following structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The coroots supplied by [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]] are in bijection with the roots and satisfy $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. This quadruple is a reduced root datum in the sense of [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], its Weyl group is canonically $W(G,T)$, and $\Delta(B)$ is a base whose nonnegative integral combinations recover $\Phi^+(B)$ ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Its semisimple rank is $|\Delta|=\operatorname{rank}G-\dim Z(G)$, and $G$ is semisimple exactly when $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X(T)$ ([[lem-reductive-center-radical-and-semisimple-quotient]]).

The isomorphism class of the unbased root datum is independent of the split Borel pair, but it is not asserted to have a unique abstract isomorphism: Weyl automorphisms already refute that assertion in type $A_1$. For two fixed split Borel pairs $(B,T),(B',T')$, conjugation by $g\in G(k)$ carrying the first pair to the second induces a canonical comparison of their **based** root data. If $g'$ is another such element, $g^{-1}g'$ lies in $N_G(B)\cap N_G(T)=B\cap N_G(T)=T$, by Borel self-normality and the Weyl/Borel correspondence. Conjugation by $T$ acts trivially on its character and cocharacter lattices and preserves the root-coroot labels, so the two induced comparisons agree. Thus uniqueness applies to the comparison attached to the fixed based pairs, while the unbased datum is defined up to isomorphism class. ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-cartan-subgroups-conjugacy-and-density]])

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup, $U=B_u$, $W=N_G(T)/T$, and choose representatives $n_w\in N_G(T)(k)$ ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) the double cosets $Bn_wB$ depend only on $w$, are smooth locally closed subvarieties of $G$, and $G$ is their disjoint union, $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}Bn_wB=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}U^wn_wB$; (b) for every $w$ the multiplication map $U^w\times B\to Bn_wB$ is an isomorphism, and $G/B=\bigsqcup_wY(w)$ with $Y(w)=UwB/B\cong\mathbf A^{n(w)}$ an affine space of dimension $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|$; (c) the **big cell** $B^-B=U^-TB$ (with $B^-$ the opposite Borel, $B^-\cap B=T$ and $U^-=B^-_u$) is open and dense in $G$, the multiplication map $U^-\times T\times U\to G$ is an open immersion, the open dense longest Bruhat cell is $Bn_{w_0}B=n_{w_0}(B^-B)$, a translate of this opposite big cell. Its flag cell $Y(w_0)$ is the unique flag cell of maximal dimension $|\Phi^+|$, while the group cell has dimension $\dim G$; (d) on $k$-points, $G(k)=\bigsqcup_wB(k)wB(k)$ is the Bruhat decomposition attached to the Tits system of [[lem-simple-reflection-double-coset-rule]], and the $G(k)$-orbits on $G/B\times G/B$ are in bijection with the $B(k)$-double cosets of $G(k)$, hence indexed by $W$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field. (a) A smooth complete connected curve $C$ over $k$ with a $k$-point that becomes isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$ over $k^{\mathrm a}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$. (b) A smooth complete geometrically connected curve with a $k$-point, homogeneous under a smooth connected affine algebraic group, is isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$, and $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf P^1)=\operatorname{PGL}_2$ as $k$-group schemes via the action on lines through the standard representation, the action being faithful with all automorphisms induced by $\operatorname{PGL}_2$. (c) For a finite-dimensional representation $(V,r)$ of a torus $T$ ([[def-group-of-multiplicative-type-and-torus]]) with weight decomposition $V=\bigoplus_i V_{\chi_i}$, the fixed points of $T$ on $\mathbf P(V)$ are the lines spanned by eigenvectors; if $T=\mathbf G_m$ and each nonzero weight space is one-dimensional, then $\mathbf P(V)^{\mathbf G_m}$ is finite and constant, and the closure of a non-fixed orbit has exactly two fixed points, namely the limits $\lim_{t\to0}tx$ and $\lim_{t\to\infty}tx$.

operations.old_value: The claim that every finite-dimensional rational representation of a split reductive group is semisimple is false. For every prime $p$ the following is a counterexample ([[thm-complete-reducibility-of-rational-modules-in-characteristic-zero]]). Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p$ and let $G=\mathrm{SL}_2$ act on $V=S^p(k^2)$, the symmetric power of the standard two-dimensional representation, with $T_2$ acting through the characters $p,p-2,\dots,-p$ ([[lem-sl2-structure-and-root-coordinates]], [[ex-fundamental-sl2-modules-in-characteristic-p]]). Let $W\subseteq V$ be the span of $e_1^p$ and $e_2^p$. Then $W$ is a two-dimensional simple submodule (the Frobenius twist of $L(1)$), every simple submodule of $V$ equals $W$, so the socle of $V$ is $W$, and $\dim_kV=p+1>2$. Hence $V$ is a nonsemisimple finite-dimensional rational representation of the split reductive group $\mathrm{SL}_2$, even though the dominant weights still classify the simple rational representations ([[thm-dominant-weights-classify-simple-rational-modules-for-split-reductive-groups]]).

operations.old_value: Write $g e_1=a e_1+c e_2$, $g e_2=b e_1+d e_2$ with $ad-bc=1$. Since $\binom pi\equiv0\pmod p$ for $0<i<p$, one has $g\cdot e_1^p=(g e_1)^p=a^p e_1^p+c^p e_2^p$ and similarly for $e_2^p$, so $W$ is a submodule; its weights $\pm p$ are distinct and nonzero, and applying the reflection matrix shows $G\cdot e_1^p=W$, so $W$ is simple. A weight vector of $V$ is a monomial $e_1^ae_2^{p-a}$ and the weight spaces are one-dimensional with distinct weights; for $0<a<p$, the upper unipotent group sends $e_1^ae_2^{p-a}$ to itself plus the nonzero multiple $a\,e_1^{a+1}e_2^{p-a-1}\cdot c$ of a different weight, so the only primitive vectors in $V$ are the nonzero multiples of $e_1^p$ and $e_2^p$. By [[thm-simple-rational-representations-have-a-highest-weight]] every simple submodule contains a primitive vector, hence is contained in $W$; as $W$ is simple, $W$ is the unique simple submodule and the socle of $V$. Since $\dim V=p+1>2$, $V$ is not a sum of simple submodules, so it is not semisimple. The classification of simple modules is unaffected because it classifies simple modules only.

particular $\dim_kL(m)\le m+1$. If $p=\operatorname{char}(k)>0$, the vectors
$e_1^p,e_2^p$ span a two-dimensional simple submodule of the symmetric power
$S^p(k^2)$ with highest weight $p\chi$, so this submodule is isomorphic to
$L(p)$, realized as the Frobenius twist of the standard module $L(1)$ through
$g\cdot e_i^p=(g\cdot e_i)^p$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
simple rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ with Borel
subgroup $B\supseteq T$ ([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]], [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a)
$V$ contains a primitive vector $v$, and it is unique up to multiplication by a
nonzero scalar; (b) its weight $\lambda$ is dominant and the weight space
$V_\lambda=kv$ is one-dimensional; (c) every weight $\mu$ of $V$ satisfies
$\mu\le\lambda$, i.e. $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\ge0$; (d) any two primitive vectors of $V$ have the same weight; this
weight is called the **highest weight** of $V$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup with
unipotent radical $U=B_u$ and roots $\Phi$
([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]],
[[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Let $(V,r)$ be a rational
representation
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). A
nonzero vector $v\in V$ is **primitive** (for the pair $(B,T)$) if it spans a
$B$-stable line. Such a vector is fixed by $U$ and is a $T$-eigenvector: the action on its one-dimensional line restricts to a character of $T$, and unipotence forces the action of $U$ on that line to be trivial. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the cited split-Borel structure, the converse holds as well: a nonzero $U$-fixed $T$-eigenvector is primitive.
The **weight** of a primitive vector is the character $\lambda\in X(T)$ with
$t\cdot v=\lambda(t)v$ for all $t$ and all $k$-algebras; for a finite-dimensional
$V$ it is the weight $\lambda$ with $v\in V_\lambda$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field, $T_2$ the diagonal torus of $\mathrm{SL}_2$, $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$ ([[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]], [[def-morphism-and-closed-subgroup-scheme]]). Then: (a) $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ are perfect; (b) the isomorphisms $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$ and $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$ satisfy $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $tu_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=u_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$ for $t=\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})$ and the root $\alpha(t)=x^2$; (c) $n_\alpha=u_\alpha(1)u_{-\alpha}(-1)u_\alpha(1)=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents the nontrivial element $s_\alpha$ of $W(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$, $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$, and $s_\alpha$ acts on $X(T_2)$ by $\chi\mapsto\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ with $\alpha^\vee=\operatorname{id}$; (d) the natural surjection $\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2$ is a central isogeny with kernel $\mu_2$, $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is simply connected, and every automorphism of $(\mathrm{SL}_2,T_2)$ maps $U^+$ to $U^+$ or $U^-$ and is determined by its restrictions to $T_2$ and $U^+$.

For a vector space $V$, let $J$ be the two-sided ideal of $T(V)$ generated by

$$v\otimes w-w\otimes v\qquad(v,w\in V).$$

The **symmetric algebra** of $V$ is the commutative graded algebra

$$S(V)=T(V)/J.$$

The quotient is commutative because its degree-one generators commute, and
all elements are sums of products of those generators. Since the relators are
homogeneous of degree two, $J$ is homogeneous. In degree $n$, the relation
space is generated by adjacent-transposition differences: an arbitrary
permutation difference is a telescoping sum along adjacent transpositions,
and each adjacent difference is a degree-$n$ multiple of a generator of $J$.
Thus the degree-$n$ piece is the quotient of $V^{\otimes n}$ by the span of
$t-\sigma(t)$ for $t\in V^{\otimes n}$ and $\sigma\in S_n$. The degree-zero
unit is the image of $1\in k$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ with Weyl
group $W$ and root datum $(X,\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$, $X=X(T)$, and let
$B\supseteq T$ be a Borel subgroup with system of positive roots $\Phi^+$ and
base $\Delta$
([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]). For a rational
representation $(V,r)$ of $G$
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]) the
$T$-weight decomposition is $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in X}V_\chi$ with
$V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(v)=v\otimes e_\chi\}$
([[lem-representations-of-diagonalizable-groups-are-sums-of-eigenspaces]]); the
**weights** of $(V,r)$ are the characters $\chi$ with $V_\chi\ne0$, and
$V_\chi$ is the **weight space** of $\chi$. An element $\lambda\in X$ is
**dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$ for every
$\alpha\in\Phi^+$ (equivalently, for every $\alpha\in\Delta$); write $X^+$ for
the set of dominant weights. Define a partial order on $X$ by $\lambda\ge\mu$ if
and only if
$\lambda-\mu=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The **fundamental weights** $\omega_i$
($i\in\Delta$) are the elements of $X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ dual to the
simple coroots, $\langle\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=\delta_{ij}$; they form a
basis of the weight lattice part and every $\lambda\in X\otimes\mathbb Q$
decomposes as
$\lambda=\sum_i\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\omega_i+\lambda_0$ with
$\lambda_0$ pairing to $0$ with every coroot
([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]).

Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]) with coordinate Hopf algebra $(A,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ ([[def-coordinate-hopf-algebra-of-affine-group-scheme]]), and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]).

(a) For a commutative unital $k$-algebra $R$ put $V_R=V\otimes_kR$ and $\operatorname{GL}_V(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]); a **rational representation** of $G$ on $V$ is a morphism of group functors $r\colon G\to\operatorname{GL}_V$, that is, a natural family of group homomorphisms $G(R)\to\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ in $R$. When $V$ is finite dimensional, a choice of basis identifies $\operatorname{GL}_V$ with the group scheme $\operatorname{GL}_n$ of [[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]].

(b) An **$A$-comodule structure** on $V$ is a $k$-linear map $\rho\colon V\to V\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]) with
$$(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id}_A)\rho=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\Delta)\rho,\qquad(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\varepsilon)\rho=\operatorname{id}_V;$$
a subspace $W\subseteq V$ is a **subcomodule** if $\rho(W)\subseteq W\otimes_kA$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

(c) The two notions correspond: a comodule structure $\rho$ gives the representation by $r_R(g)(v\otimes1)=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes g)\rho(v)$, extended $R$-linearly, and this assignment is a bijection onto the rational representations of $G$ on $V$ under which subcomodules correspond to subrepresentations; the proof is [[lem-representations-of-affine-group-schemes-are-comodules]].

(d) The coaction $\Delta\colon A\to A\otimes_kA$ makes $A$ itself an $A$-comodule, the **regular representation** of $G$. A representation $r$ is **faithful** if every $r_R$ is injective.

The axioms in (b) are exactly the two comodule diagrams; no smoothness, reducedness or finite-dimensionality of $V$ is imposed, and a basis of $V$ is chosen only to name the matrix group $\operatorname{GL}_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a
split reductive group over a field $k$, let $B\supseteq T$ be a Borel subgroup,
and let $X(T)^+$ be the set of dominant characters of the maximal torus $T$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]]). For every
$\lambda\in X(T)^+$ there exists a simple rational representation $V(\lambda)$
of $G$, unique up to isomorphism, whose $T$-weight decomposition is
$$V(\lambda)=V(\lambda)_\lambda\oplus\bigoplus_{\mu<\lambda}V(\lambda)_\mu$$
with $\dim_kV(\lambda)_\lambda=1$, and every simple rational representation of
$G$ is isomorphic to $V(\lambda)$ for a unique $\lambda\in X(T)^+$
([[thm-simple-rational-representations-have-a-highest-weight]],
[[thm-simple-modules-with-equal-highest-weight-are-isomorphic]],
[[lem-dominant-characters-arise-as-primitive-weights-for-split-reductive-groups]]).
The map sending a simple representation to its highest weight is a bijection
from the set of isomorphism classes of simple rational representations of $G$
to $X(T)^+$; it holds in every characteristic.

derivations.claim: The basis monomials $e_1^ae_2^{p-a}$ of $V$ are $T_2$-eigenvectors of weights $(2a-p)\chi$ for $a=0,\dots,p$, i.e. of the characters $-p,-p+2,\dots,p$; each weight space of $V$ is therefore one-dimensional and spanned by a single monomial, and $T_2$ acts through the characters $p,p-2,\dots,-p$ as claimed.

The primitive vectors of $V$ are exactly the nonzero multiples of $e_1^p$. Indeed, a primitive vector is a nonzero $T_2$-eigenvector fixed by $U^+$ ([[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]], [[def-primitive-vector-of-a-rational-representation]]), hence by step 1.1 is a nonzero multiple of some monomial $m_a=e_1^ae_2^{p-a}$; and $u_\alpha(t)\cdot m_a=e_1^a(e_2+te_1)^{p-a}$ has, as the coefficient of $e_1^p$, the term $t^{p-a}$ (the $i=p-a$ summand, with binomial coefficient $1$). If $a<p$, the original monomial has zero coefficient of $e_1^p$, whereas the translated coefficient is the nonzero polynomial $t^{p-a}$ in $k[t]$. Thus fixedness over every base algebra excludes $a<p$. For $a=p$, $u_\alpha(t)\cdot e_1^p=e_1^p$ for all $t$, so $e_1^p$ is fixed.

Let $S\subseteq V$ be a nonzero submodule; if $S$ is simple, then by [F2] it contains a primitive vector $v$, which by step 2.1 is a nonzero multiple of $e_1^p$; hence $e_1^p\in S$. By [F1] the $G$-submodule generated by $e_1^p$ is $W$ (it is nonzero and contained in the simple module $W$), so $W\subseteq S$, and simplicity of $S$ gives $S=W$. Therefore $W$ is the unique simple submodule of $V$ and the socle of $V$ is $W$. Since $\dim_kV=p+1$ while $\dim_kW=2$, a semisimple $V$ would be the sum of its simple submodules, namely $W$, which is impossible; hence $V$ is not semisimple.

The representation $V=S^p(k^2)$ is finite-dimensional and rational, $G=\mathrm{SL}_2$ is a split reductive group of characteristic $p$, and $V$ is not semisimple by step 3.1, while its simple submodules and those of every rational $G$-module are still classified by the dominant weights by [F4]. This refutes the claim that every finite-dimensional rational representation of a split reductive group is semisimple.

Let $k$ be a field and let $G$ be an affine algebraic group over $k$, that is, an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-affine-scheme]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]).

**(a) Unipotent representations.** A finite-dimensional rational representation $(V,r,\rho)$ of $G$ ([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]], [[def-vector-space]]) is **unipotent** if there is a $k$-basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) in which every operator $r(g)$ is upper triangular with all diagonal entries equal to $1$. Equivalently, by the comodule dictionary, $V$ is unipotent if and only if $V$ has a complete $G$-stable flag
$$V=V_m\supseteq V_{m-1}\supseteq\dots\supseteq V_0=0$$
with $G$ acting trivially on each quotient $V_i/V_{i-1}$; the equivalence uses that a complete flag with trivial successive quotients is exactly a chain of subspaces in a basis as above, and conversely.

**(b) Unipotent groups.** The group $G$ is **unipotent** if every nonzero rational representation of $G$ has a nonzero $G$-fixed vector, equivalently if every simple rational representation of $G$ is one-dimensional with trivial action. Because every rational representation is a union of finite-dimensional subrepresentations ([[lem-finite-dimensional-subcomodules-contain-elements]]), it suffices to test finite-dimensional representations: $G$ is unipotent if and only if every nonzero finite-dimensional rational representation has a nonzero fixed vector.

No smoothness, reducedness or connectedness of $G$ is imposed, and $G$ is not assumed affine over the base beyond the standing hypothesis of this definition; the matrix formulation in (a) is written out because the group scheme $U_n$ of upper unitriangular matrices is introduced separately and is not used in the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup with base $\Delta$, and let $W$, $\Phi^+$ be as above ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). (a) For every subset $I\subseteq\Delta$ there is a unique smooth parabolic subgroup $P_I\subseteq G$ containing $B$ with $P_I=\bigsqcup_{w\in W_I}C(w)$, where $C(w)=BwB$; the correspondence $I\mapsto P_I$ is a bijection onto the set of smooth parabolic subgroup varieties of $G$ containing $B$, and the standard parabolic subgroups are exactly the groups $P_G(\lambda)$ for cocharacters $\lambda$ with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\ge0$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, with $I=\{\alpha\in\Delta:\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle=0\}$. (b) The unipotent radical of $P_I$ is $R_u(P_I)=U_I:=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+\smallsetminus\Phi_I}U_\alpha$, directly spanned in any order, and the multiplication map $R_u(P_I)\rtimes L_I\to P_I$ is a group-scheme isomorphism (Levi decomposition), with $L_I$ the standard Levi subgroup of [[lem-standard-levi-subgroup]]. (c) Every smooth parabolic subgroup of $G$ containing $B$ is $P_I$ for a unique $I$, and over an algebraically closed field every smooth parabolic subgroup of $G$ is conjugate by an element of $G(k)$ to a unique standard parabolic $P_I$. (d) $P_\varnothing=B$ and $P_\Delta=G$.


The general proper-quotient Definition still permits nonsmooth parabolic subgroup schemes; the standard classification above is restricted to smooth subgroup varieties. For example, in characteristic $p$, the Frobenius preimage $F_{\mathrm{SL}_2}^{-1}(B^{(p)})$ is nonsmooth, contains $B$, and has proper quotient $\mathbf P^{1,(p)}$, so it is not one of these smooth $P_I$.

Then: (a) $L_I$ is smooth connected reductive with maximal torus $T$, root system $\Phi_I$ and root datum $(X(T),\Phi_I,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$, and Weyl group $W_I$; the root groups of $L_I$ are exactly the $U_\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\Phi_I$; (b) $T_I$ is the largest subtorus of $T$ killed by all $\alpha\in I$, and $L_I$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\Phi_I$; (c) $B\cap L_I$ is a Borel subgroup $B_I$ of $L_I$ with positive system $\Phi_I\cap\Phi^+(B)$ and base $I$; (d) for each $\alpha\in\Delta$, choose a rational fundamental dual vector $\eta_\alpha\in X_*(T)\otimes\mathbb Q$ with $\langle\beta,\eta_\alpha\rangle=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$, and let $\lambda_\alpha$ be any positive integral multiple lying in $X_*(T)$. For every $\beta\in\Delta\smallsetminus\{\alpha\}$, every representative of $s_\beta$ in $N_G(T)(k)$ lies in $P_G(\lambda_\alpha)(k)$, and this subgroup contains $G_\beta$. Rational dual vectors need not themselves be integral cocharacters; a possible central component does not change the parabolic.

A closed subgroup scheme $P\subseteq G$ is a **parabolic subgroup** if the fppf quotient $G/P$ is representable and proper over $k$, equivalently if $G/P$ is complete ([[thm-homogeneous-space-for-smooth-affine-group]], [[def-proper-morphism]], [[def-complete-variety]]). The **unipotent radical** $R_u(P)\subseteq P$ is the largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup ([[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]]), the **radical** $R(P)$ is the largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup ([[def-derived-subgroup-and-solvable-algebraic-group]], [[def-radical-and-unipotent-radical-of-an-algebraic-group]]), and a **Levi subgroup** of $P$ is a smooth closed subgroup $L\subseteq P$ such that the multiplication map $L\ltimes R_u(P)\to P$ is an isomorphism. The conditional proper-quotient definition above uses no choice principle. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the following supplemental representability and structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Representability of $G/P$ is a theorem for smooth affine $G$ and closed $P$ ([[thm-homogeneous-space-for-smooth-affine-group]]); properness of a representable quotient is equivalent to completeness by definition, which is the form used in the propositions below. The definition does not assume $P$ smooth or connected; in a smooth connected affine group such a parabolic is connected and self-normalizing by [[thm-solvable-subgroups-and-the-radical-as-borel-intersection]]. Smooth parabolic subgroup varieties form the class to which the standard $P_I$ and Levi classification below applies; nonsmooth Frobenius-thickened proper-quotient subgroups are retained by this general definition. The definition makes no reference to split reductive structure, so that the standard-parabolic theory can establish the equivalence for smooth subgroup varieties. In the Levi decomposition below the subgroup $L$ is required only to be smooth and closed; when $P$ is smooth, its unipotent radical is smooth and the product decomposition is a statement about schemes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(G,T)$ a root ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ is a split reductive subgroup of semisimple rank $1$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}=1$, and the rational multiples of $\alpha$ occurring in $\Phi$ are only $\pm\alpha$; (b) the root group $U_\alpha$ is $T$-stable, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$, and has $\operatorname{Lie}(U_\alpha)=\mathfrak g_\alpha$; a smooth $T$-stable subgroup $H\subseteq G$ contains $U_\alpha$ iff $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\supseteq\mathfrak g_\alpha$; (c) $W(G_\alpha,T)=\{1,s_\alpha\}$ with the nontrivial element represented by some $n_\alpha\in N_{G_\alpha}(T)(k)$, and there is a unique cocharacter $\alpha^\vee\in X_*(T)$ with $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ for all $x\in X(T)$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; (d) $G$ is generated by $T$ and the root groups $U_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; (e) $(X(T),\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ is a reduced root datum and $W(G,T)$ coincides with the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(X(T))$ generated by the $s_\alpha$; (f) for a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with positive system $\Phi^+$, the multiplication map $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}U_\alpha\to B_u=R_u(B)$ is a $T$-equivariant isomorphism of varieties for any ordering of $\Phi^+$, every smooth $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ is the product of the $U_\alpha$ it contains, and a subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi^+$ is the weight set of a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup of $B_u$ iff it is quasi-closed. Here quasi-closed means that for $\alpha,\beta\in\Psi$ and integers $i,j>0$, every root $i\alpha+j\beta$ whose Chevalley commutator coefficient $N_{\alpha,\beta;i,j}$ is nonzero in $k$ lies in $\Psi$. Every closed subset of $\Phi^+$ satisfies this condition; in characteristic $0$ or characteristic $p>3$, quasi-closure is equivalent to ordinary root closure, namely closure under sums that are roots.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be an
affine group scheme of finite type over a field $k$ and let $H\subseteq G$ be a
closed subgroup scheme. Then there exist a finite-dimensional rational
representation $(V,r)$ of $G$ and a line $L\subseteq V$ such that
$H=\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$ scheme-theoretically: for every $k$-algebra $R$,
$\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)(R)=\{g\in G(R):gL_R=L_R\}$
([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]],
[[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]).
Moreover, if $L=kv$ then
$\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\{x\in\operatorname{Lie}(G):xv\in kv\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ (not necessarily
finite-dimensional) that is generated as a $G$-module by a primitive vector $v$
of weight $\lambda$
([[def-primitive-vector-of-a-rational-representation]]). Then: (a) $V$ is
generated as a module over the opposite unipotent group $U^-$ by $v$; (b)
$V=kv\oplus\bigoplus_{\mu<\lambda}V_\mu$, where every weight $\mu$ of $V$ has
the form $\mu=\lambda-\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}m_\alpha\alpha$ with
$m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and $V_\lambda=kv$ has dimension one; (c)
$\lambda$ is dominant; (d) the sum of all proper $G$-stable subspaces of $V$ is
proper, so $V$ has a largest proper $G$-submodule and the quotient by it is a
simple $G$-module generated by the image of $v$.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group, $B\supseteq T$ a Borel subgroup with
unipotent radical $U=B_u$ and roots $\Phi$
([[def-borel-subgroup-and-maximal-torus]],
[[def-unipotent-algebraic-group]],
[[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]],
[[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Let $(V,r)$ be a rational
representation
([[def-rational-representation-and-comodule-of-an-affine-group-scheme]]). A
nonzero vector $v\in V$ is **primitive** (for the pair $(B,T)$) if it spans a
$B$-stable line. Such a vector is fixed by $U$ and is a $T$-eigenvector: the action on its one-dimensional line restricts to a character of $T$, and unipotence forces the action of $U$ on that line to be trivial. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the cited split-Borel structure, the converse holds as well: a nonzero $U$-fixed $T$-eigenvector is primitive.
The **weight** of a primitive vector is the character $\lambda\in X(T)$ with
$t\cdot v=\lambda(t)v$ for all $t$ and all $k$-algebras; for a finite-dimensional
$V$ it is the weight $\lambda$ with $v\in V_\lambda$
([[def-weight-and-dominant-weight-of-a-rational-representation]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(V,r)$ be a
rational representation of a split reductive group $(G,T)$ and let
$n\in N_G(T)(R)$ for a $k$-algebra $R$. If $v\in V_\lambda$, then $n\cdot(v\otimes1)\in(V\otimes_kR)_{n\lambda}$, where $n\lambda:T_R\to\mathbf G_{m,R}$ is the character $t\mapsto\lambda(n^{-1}tn)$, tested over every $R$-algebra. If $R$ is disconnected, this character can vary between components; the target denotes its eigensubmodule over $R$. Consequently, for every $w\in W(G,T)$ the weight spaces
$V_\lambda$ and $V_{w\lambda}$ have the same dimension, and the set of weights
of $(V,r)$ is stable under $W$
([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]],
[[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ with root datum $(X,\Phi,\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee)$ ([[def-roots-and-root-groups-of-a-split-reductive-group]]). Then: (a) $W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T$ is a finite constant group scheme and $W(G,T)(k')=N_G(T)(k')/T(k')$ for every field $k'\supseteq k$; (b) every split maximal torus of $G$ lies in a Borel subgroup, and every Borel subgroup of $G$ containing $T$ is of the form $P_G(\lambda)$ for a regular cocharacter $\lambda$, hence is split; (c) $W(G,T)$ acts simply transitively on the finite set of Borel subgroups of $G$ containing $T$, and the map sending a Borel subgroup to its system of positive roots is a bijection onto the set of positive systems; (d) there is a canonical isomorphism $W(G,T)\cong W(R)$ of finite groups, and $W(G,T)$ is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$, for any base $\Delta$; (e) for $w\in W(G,T)$ and a representative $n_w\in N_G(T)(k)$, the double coset $Bn_wB$ depends only on $w$ and $n_wU_\alpha n_w^{-1}=U_{w\alpha}$ for all roots $\alpha$.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Let $(G,T)$ be a split reductive group over $k$ ([[def-split-reductive-algebraic-group]]). Its **root datum** is the quadruple
$$R(G,T)=(X(T),\Phi(G,T),X_*(T),\Phi^\vee(G,T)),$$
where the character and cocharacter lattices are those of [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]], the roots are the nonzero adjoint characters, and $\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ consists of the associated coroots. Its **rank** is $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}X(T)=\dim T$. For a split Borel pair $(B,T)$, its base $\Delta(B)$ consists of roots in $\Phi^+(B)$ that are not sums of two positive roots; the pair gives the based root datum $(R(G,T),\Delta(B))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the root-group, Weyl and centre suppliers for the following structural assertions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The coroots supplied by [[thm-root-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group]] are in bijection with the roots and satisfy $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. This quadruple is a reduced root datum in the sense of [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], its Weyl group is canonically $W(G,T)$, and $\Delta(B)$ is a base whose nonnegative integral combinations recover $\Phi^+(B)$ ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Its semisimple rank is $|\Delta|=\operatorname{rank}G-\dim Z(G)$, and $G$ is semisimple exactly when $\mathbb Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X(T)$ ([[lem-reductive-center-radical-and-semisimple-quotient]]).

The isomorphism class of the unbased root datum is independent of the split Borel pair, but it is not asserted to have a unique abstract isomorphism: Weyl automorphisms already refute that assertion in type $A_1$. For two fixed split Borel pairs $(B,T),(B',T')$, conjugation by $g\in G(k)$ carrying the first pair to the second induces a canonical comparison of their **based** root data. If $g'$ is another such element, $g^{-1}g'$ lies in $N_G(B)\cap N_G(T)=B\cap N_G(T)=T$, by Borel self-normality and the Weyl/Borel correspondence. Conjugation by $T$ acts trivially on its character and cocharacter lattices and preserves the root-coroot labels, so the two induced comparisons agree. Thus uniqueness applies to the comparison attached to the fixed based pairs, while the unbased datum is defined up to isomorphism class. ([[thm-weyl-group-borel-chambers]], [[lem-cartan-subgroups-conjugacy-and-density]])

derivations.claim: Let $(V,L)$ be as in [F2] and let $v\ne0$ generate $L$. Since $P_i\supseteq B\supseteq U$ and $P_i\supseteq T$, the line $L$ is $B$-stable, so $v$ is primitive; let $\lambda_i$ be its weight. Replacing $V$ by the $G$-submodule generated by $v$ does not change the line $L$, and by [F3] the weight $\lambda_i$ is then dominant.

For $j\ne i$ choose a representative $n\in P_i(k)$ of the simple reflection $s_{\alpha_j}$, which exists because $P_i$ contains $U_{\pm\alpha_j}$ and $T$ by [F1]. Since $n$ stabilizes $L$, the vector $n\cdot v$ is a nonzero multiple of $v$, hence has weight $\lambda_i$; on the other hand by [F4] it has weight $s_{\alpha_j}(\lambda_i)=\lambda_i-\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\alpha_j$. Therefore $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\alpha_j=0$ and $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=0$.

For the remaining index, suppose $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0$. Then $s_{\alpha_i}$ fixes $\lambda_i$; choose a representative $n_i\in N_G(T)(k)$ of this simple reflection. It takes $v$ to a nonzero vector of weight $s_{\alpha_i}(\lambda_i)=\lambda_i$. By [F3], the weight-$\lambda_i$ space in the module generated by $v$ is one-dimensional, so $n_i v$ is a nonzero multiple of $v$ and $n_i$ stabilizes $L$. Since $\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)=P_i$, this gives $n_i\in P_i$. But $U_{\alpha_i}\subseteq B\subseteq P_i$, and conjugation by $n_i$ carries $U_{\alpha_i}$ onto $U_{-\alpha_i}$; this contradicts [F1], which says $U_{-\alpha_i}\not\subseteq P_i$. Thus $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\ne0$, and dominance gives $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0$.

If the root datum is semisimple, then by [F6] the element $\lambda_i$ has the unique expression $\sum_j\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\omega_j$ in the basis of fundamental weights; by steps 2.1 and 2.2 only the $i$-th coefficient is nonzero, so $\lambda_i=\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\omega_i$ with $\langle\lambda_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0$.
Steps 1.1 to 2.1 produce, for each $i\in I$, a finite-dimensional representation and a primitive vector with the required pairings, and the stated semisimple form of the weight.
